tip: Confirm the Katana holder and target with every living teammate each night, and assign any role-block around the attack plan. A coordinated block can make a later attack succeed where an earlier one failed.
Keep a consistent public rationale for your votes, but don’t automatically vote as a bloc. A well-explained vote against a teammate can preserve your credibility if the teammate is later exposed.
Treat a dead teammate’s last will as a major risk: it can name surviving teammates directly. Don’t assume distancing or earlier cooperation will prevent a teammate from exposing you after death.

A failed attack is evidence that the target may have had protection, not proof of who protected them. Reassess the target and possible protectors before trying again; consider changing timing or stopping the likely protection first.

Before treating an optional action as proof, check whether the rules make it mandatory. Medic and other night actions are optional, so a skipped night is not a contradiction; several accusations this game collapsed on that misreading.

Run the count checks. An Archivist sample or Surveyor group should be checked against the living-player count at the time, and vote totals against the number of voters, before using them to hang someone.
Vote as a block only when unavoidable. Yes-on-a-doomed-teammate and shared Innocent votes on the same trials exposed Mallory and Niaj and made the Village's alignment reads easy.
Ask a claimant for a concrete, checkable detail before voting, and separate a claim's consistency from its proof. Repeated accusations without new evidence drove several hangs of innocent players.
Protection gives no feedback, so say only that your protection is consistent with the target's survival; competing Medic claims were hard to resolve without corroboration.

Choose a claim before it is forced, and keep your public claim, will, and later answers consistent. A Vanilla claim is not automatically safe: roles with tokens can be exposed by an Accountant’s count, so have a plausible explanation for what that check could show.

A doubled trial vote is visible in the announced total, and the revealed votes narrow down which side supplied the extra vote. Avoid making your trial votes point in different directions across manipulated trials; plan how each vote will look alongside your claim and teammates’ votes.

Treat a failed Katana attack as evidence that the target may have been protected. Change targets or remove a likely protector rather than blindly retrying; keep the holder, target, and any role-block coordinated in night chat.

Track trial votes across flips, not just individual statements. Repeatedly sparing teammates who later flip Yakuza can become strong alignment evidence, especially when it forms a pattern with other votes.

Separate what a result proves from what it merely suggests: a Tracker confirms a visit, not the action; a token count is not an exact-role check; and a skipped action is not a contradiction when actions are optional. Treat roles as unique only when the rules say they are.
Report the exact surveyed group and the anonymous role result, and preserve both in your will. The result narrows the possibilities to that group but does not identify which member has the role.

Use vote-count anomalies as cumulative evidence. Compare who voted which way across manipulated trials, token counts, and later role flips; one extra vote or one token count alone does not identify the manipulator.

Keep a compact record of trial votes and revisit it after flips. Repeatedly sparing players who later flip Yakuza is meaningful alignment evidence, but weigh it alongside each player's stated reasoning rather than treating one dissenting vote as proof.

Before voting on a claimed role, check whether the claim's mechanical premises are actually possible (e.g. whether an optional action is treated as mandatory). Overclaimed rules made Erin look worse than her evidence warranted; verify the rule text before pressing a case.

Keep a running tally of each night's visits, blocks and deaths and cross-check claims against it daily. Judy's and Niaj's competing Medic claims stayed unresolved for days because nobody tracked who was blocked or who visited whom on each night.

A Ballot Stuffer's doubled vote shows up as a vote-count mismatch. Use the announced totals to identify the manipulator, and treat the Innocent voters on a trial with a mismatch as the candidates to check.

Yakuza with a Pharmacist or Katana should vary attack targets and avoid repeatedly blocking or attacking the same suspected protector, since the Medic claims and Tracker results made the pattern easy for Village to read.

When a lone player is the only living voter to spare a confirmed Yakuza, flag it early but check whether the teammate's own claimed history is verifiable before using it as a trial basis; repeated trials on weak evidence left the Village too few voters to act on the right case.

Medic protection is optional but a nightly Medic who skips visits looks suspicious; if you protect, log every target and any tokens spent in your will so later claims can be cross-checked against your own record.
Avoid voting Innocent on a teammate at multiple trials in a row; the pattern of sparing the same Yakuza became the strongest alignment read and got the Pharmacist executed.

Don't name your fellow Yakuza in your will or leave a Grunt-naming trail; a dying Pharmacist's will named a teammate and sent the village straight to a trial that killed a real Village-aligned player.

Track Ballot Stuffer effects: when announced trial totals exceed the living voter count, the extra vote is a hidden Innocent or Guilty; use this to find the stuffing voter's bloc rather than hanging on a single vote.

Before trials, separate claims that are checkable (Tracker visits, Accountant counts) from unverifiable claims (Archivist samples, Medic protections); a sample that names no one cannot clear or convict anyone, so don't let it drive hangings.

Choose eavesdrop targets who are likely to send private messages (active Yakuza-suspect or coordinating players) rather than quiet ones; four of my six reads were empty, so the role gave little information when I watched players who rarely PM.

Track the public claims against the mechanical facts (who visited whom, token counts, the exact count of living players) before voting; several trials were driven by unverifiable archive or Medic claims while a simple headcount or visit record could have settled them.

Do not hang on a single voting pattern after a teammate's accusation; when a Yakuza will names you, weigh it against your own checkable history, and avoid joining a pile-on from one flagged voter without asking for a second independent check.
Avoid voting Innocent as a bloc with an exposed teammate across several trials; the repeated pattern of sparing confirmed Yakuza is what made the survivors hang the last Yakuza.

Medic protection is optional each night, and two Medics can both claim the same target; a skipped or same-target night is not a contradiction on its own, so ask for exact targets and the role's feedback limits rather than treating silence as proof.

Separate an action being optional from a role being unable to perform it. A Tracker reporting no visit can make a Medic claim less persuasive, but it does not contradict the claim; likewise, don't treat two players claiming the same role as impossible unless the rules say the role is unique.

A token count is not an exact-role or alignment check. Work out what token uses could explain the count, then combine it with independent evidence. Vote-total discrepancies can narrow down who might have manipulated a trial, but the extra vote alone does not identify its owner.

Keep information-seeking votes separate from guilt judgments. When a trial vote is justified as a way to hear someone out, say so clearly—and at the verdict, assess the evidence for guilt rather than treating the earlier Yes vote as proof.

Before voting on an unverifiable role claim, ask for a specific, checkable detail (a target, a result, a date) and track whether the claimant's later statements stay consistent with their earlier ones; the Yakuza flips in this game came from claims that never got tested against the public record.

Do not let your teammate's late accusation be the decisive reason you vote; a teammate who has been exposed or is about to be hanged can name you in their will. Spread your votes so you are not seen voting as a block with the same people.

Track whether a claimed Medic's protection ever showed up in a Katana result; with optional actions, a protector who claims nightly protection and skips nights is hard to test, so weight the claim by consistency across the whole game rather than one skipped night.

Post a short, consistent vote rationale every trial and keep it matching your later votes; several players here were judged on votes that looked like a bloc after the fact, and explaining a vote at the time protects you more than explaining it afterwards.

When a vote count doesn't match the revealed votes, check the arithmetic against living players before building a case on it; a miscounted archive or vote total can get a true claimant hanged or make a liar look more credible.

Use Standard protection proactively on likely kill targets, but keep your will current and never claim a save: protection gives you no feedback, and being visited or surviving does not prove protection worked.

Separate a confirmed visit from an inferred action. A Tracker can establish where someone went, not whether they protected, blocked, or attacked; likewise, an optional role's no-visit result is not a mechanical contradiction.

Use revealed vote histories as cumulative evidence, not as proof from one vote. Repeatedly sparing players who later flip Yakuza is a meaningful pattern, especially when the voter’s explanation is compared with what they said at the time.
A mismatch between announced and revealed trial totals can establish that votes were manipulated, but it does not identify whose vote was doubled. A token count is also not an exact-role check.

Before the Katana vote, confirm with teammates which member holds it and whether they have a separate action; a Pharmacist who blocks the same target every night while the Grunt holds the Katana makes the team's pattern obvious to the Village.

Don't let your teammate's Vanilla-cover or fake-role story go unchallenged for days; a claimed Medic who skips protections and a Vanilla-to-Medic switch created a loop of Village trials that protected the real Yakuza.

Voting Innocent on multiple confirmed teammates' executions is the clearest alignment tell; spread Innocent votes across trials so no single pattern exposes you, and pick a plausible reason you can repeat.

Track vote-count anomalies and token counts against claims early: a manipulated trial total or a Ballot Stuffer token can explain a flip, and the Village spent several days on unverifiable Archivist and Medic disputes instead of checking the counts.

When a Yakuza's will names a teammate, verify that teammate's claimed role history against the board before executing; Grunt-based accusations were acted on in a single day without independent evidence.

Save your one-use clean for a high-value kill that is likely to land. Cleaning only replaces the dead player's role and will; it does not prevent an attack or hide its cause. Spending it on a target who survives wastes the token.

Choose a cover that remains credible against the roles and public evidence in play. Switching from a Vanilla claim to a Medic claim invited comparison with the real Medic and the Tracker’s visit result; a fake claim can create more exposure than it conceals.

Agree on a consistent Katana plan each night, and after a failed attack, assume the target may be protected rather than blindly retrying. Shift to another valuable target or address the likely protector.

Plan teammate votes for the later record, not just the current trial. A teammate who repeatedly spares confirmed Yakuza can become an obvious suspect after flips; coordinate distancing and defense so the pattern is less revealing.

When announced trial totals don't match the revealed votes, record which side got the extra vote in each trial. Then look for the one player whose votes line up with every manipulation. Combined with a token count, this can pin down a Ballot Stuffer without any role check.
evidence: Heidi noted the extra Innocent at Carol's trial and the extra Guilty at Ivan's trial. Carol voted Innocent and Guilty respectively, and had 1 token left after N1. Carol was hanged on Day 3 and flipped Ballot Stuffer.

tip: Don't fake-claim a token role, or Vanilla while you hold tokens, when an Accountant or the real role holder may be alive. If caught, don't switch to another unique-feeling power role. Instead pick a claim whose token count and results nobody living can contradict.
evidence: Heidi's 1-token audit broke Carol's Vanilla claim. Her Archivist fallback was immediately counterclaimed by the real Archivist, Erin, which kept her under suspicion until she was hanged.

tip: Once a teammate is clearly doomed, vote Guilty with the town. Lone Innocent votes on a teammate who later flips Yakuza become the main case against you.
evidence: Mallory was the only voter besides Carol to vote Innocent at Carol's execution, and later voted Innocent on Niaj. She was nominated every day after that and hanged on Day 6. Alice voted Guilty on both Carol and Niaj and survived to the final four.

tip: Don't hang a power-role claimant just because the claim came late or is hard to verify, especially if the result fits the accused's own admissions. Ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits.
evidence: Ivan's Oracle result (Niaj is not Vanilla) was true. Alice, a Yakuza, nominated him. Judy and Bob voted Guilty, and the doubled Yakuza vote pushed it to execution. The Village lost its Oracle for nothing.

tip: Protect from Night 1 and keep guarding claimed or valuable information roles. Free Standard protection beats the Katana outright.
evidence: Judy's N1 protection saved Heidi, whose audit later cracked Carol. Her N6 protection of Erin stopped Alice's last Katana kill and gave the Village a 3-1 final day.

tip: Never name living teammates in your last will. In the endgame, kill the protector or a non-protected player rather than the player the Medic is publicly known to guard.
evidence: Mallory's will said 'Alice is our Grunt', which was the whole case that hanged Alice on Day 7. On N6, Alice attacked Erin, whom Judy had claimed protecting (N3) and protected again, so the attack failed.

tip: Use public Surveyor or partial-role results with your private knowledge to locate Neutrals and other threats.
evidence: Dave's survey group was Alice/Bob/Carol with Vulture revealed. Alice and Carol were Yakuza, so Yakuza killed Bob, the Vulture, on N3 and removed a rival win condition.

tip: Get the mechanics right before accusing someone. Night actions are optional, and counts like 'living others' include players who died that night, so check both before calling something a contradiction. A false 'contradiction' costs you credibility.
evidence: Erin claimed a Medic must act every night, Village players corrected her, and she was later nominated and tried. Mallory's claimed archive miscount was itself wrong, and Niaj and Alice publicly corrected it.

tip: Use the Diviner on the Katana holder when a Veteran or Vigilante might be alive. The Strong Defense it grants beats a Veteran's Strong counterattack, because an attack must be strictly higher than Defense to kill. Info checks on town can wait. An unprotected holder attacking a vocal organizer is exactly how a Veteran gets a free kill.

Don't send the Katana at a confident, vocal player who invites attention, especially when no Veteran has been seen. Prefer quiet targets or ones you've already scouted. If you must hit a likely power role, either protect the holder first or use a Ritualist guess (an Astral Visit, which a Veteran can't punish).

Don't have two or more teammates claim Vanilla in a power-heavy setup. One archive list or role count can show there is no Village Vanilla slot left and expose both at once. Spread fake claims over plausible unverified roles, or keep at most one Vanilla.

A doubled trial vote shows up publicly as a total that doesn't match the revealed votes. That proves a Ballot Stuffer exists and can confirm a town claim that names one, such as an Archivist list. Spend it only when it swings a trial that matters, not on trials that end Innocent anyway.

Before nominating someone who is only a soft lean, ask whether they could be a hidden information role. A trial forces their claim, and an Archivist or Seer claim mid-game can reveal the whole Yakuza lineup. It's often better to kill them quietly at night.

Diviner checks on non-Yakuza reveal exact roles, which turns the Ritualist's guesses into guaranteed, unannounced kills. Feed every Diviner result straight to the Ritualist. Pair this with the Katana for two kills a night, and save the tokens for confirmed investigators.

Before choosing a Katana target, consider a hidden Veteran: an organized-sounding vocal player may be alerting. When a player's claimed alert history changes between days, treat it as bait and never visit them. Use Astral Ritualist kills or Day hangs on suspected Veterans instead.

A Ballot Stuffer token turns a tied Guilty/Innocent vote into a guaranteed block. Spend it on days when a teammate may be tried. The rules publicly announce the extra vote, though, which can confirm an archive or claim list that names Ballot Stuffer. If that list is already public, expect the extra vote to validate it.

Multiple Yakuza all fake-claiming Vanilla is fragile against an Archivist or Surveyor. Once a role list leaks, Vanilla claims become provably impossible. Have one member fake-claim a plausible power role early, or avoid claiming at all, so the claim count doesn't expose the team.

Once you reach 2v2 at a Day, plan the endgame in night chat. Vote No on every nomination, kill one villager at night, then nominate and hang the last one at 2v1. Make sure both members submit identical Katana votes.
Avoid taking uncoordinated shots on Night 2 based on minor behavioral misreads or aggressive questioning. Hitting town information roles (like Surveyor) accelerates evil reaching vote parity.

Do not let early trials snowball on stacked soft leans and minor timeline misrememberings. Hanging an innocent Vanilla Villager on Day 2 gives evil an easy mislynch and squanders the town's numerical advantage.

When a Ballot Stuffer manipulates trial counts, calculate vote thresholds immediately. If evil reaches parity where trial votes tie (e.g. 4-4), town must coordinate night actions (like Vigilante shots) strictly on the evil bloc.

A starting investigative identity is not guaranteed in a Roleplayer setup. A Roleplayer genuinely believes their assigned role, so their false claim or results are not necessarily deliberate lies. Exact-role checks and death reveals override the identity they believed.

Repeated weak suspicions do not become independent evidence just because several players repeat them. Before executing or shooting over inaccurate statements, identify what distinguishes deliberate fabrication from corrected mistakes. Frank's execution and Erin's shooting show how costly skipping that distinction can be.

Separate an archive's valid sample size from the truth of its claimed contents. One corroborated entry does not authenticate the whole list. Once you accept the list, explicitly account for the sampled and unsampled roles before declaring that a claimed role has no remaining slot.

Calculate tomorrow's living factions before choosing an endgame shot. With seven players and an evil double vote, four ordinary Guilty votes cannot execute. Killing the Ballot Stuffer still does not restore control if simultaneous Katana and Ritualist kills leave Village at parity.

An active Ritualist makes exact-role disclosure dangerous: a correct guess enables an additional kill independently of the Katana. Reveal only when the immediate benefit justifies that risk. Private messages are not a safe workaround when a Wiretap may be alive.

applies_to: Surveyor and other investigative roles (Sheriff, Seer, Tracker, Lookout, Archivist, Accountant)
tip: Post your results publicly in your first speech after learning them, not only in your last will. A will is revealed only if you die, and by then the Village may have lost the chance to cross-check your claim against the other claimant. Erin's Night 1 survey implicated Carol as the Seer, but it stayed hidden until Erin was killed.

Before voting Guilty, require a mechanical contradiction, a verified result or a vote that clashes with a stated read. Several soft leans, a misstated timeline and pressure on a nominee are not enough. Stacked leans hanged Frank, a Vanilla Villager, on Day 2.

When two players claim the same role, check each claim against the public record: who was shot, who died to what, and whether an archive or role count is consistent. Two Vigilante claimants meant one was a fake, and Mallory's Vigilante claim was false. Check the claims before hanging anyone on the count.

Confirm a target's role before shooting, and avoid shooting a player who has announced a claim you cannot check. Niaj's Basic shot on Erin, a Surveyor, was a mistake that cost the Village an information role and let the Yakuza keep the Katana.

Before voting Guilty, ask each Yes voter to name a concrete contradiction in the defendant's own words or votes. Frank was hanged 6-5 on stacked soft leans and a nomination made 'to hear a defense'. When a nominator says they aren't committed, treat the Yes votes as pile-on, not evidence.

Don't let teammates make mutually exclusive public claims. Two living Yakuza both claiming Vanilla contradicted an Archivist's role list, which gave Village a checkable lever. Agree on the claimed role set in night chat, and have at most one teammate claim a role that can be cross-checked.

When a Ballot Stuffer may be alive, the announced vote total can exceed the number of voters. Majority is computed against the counted total, so a 4-4 split with a stuffer means no trial can reach majority. Work this out before arguing over who is Yakuza, since it decides whether a nomination can succeed at all.

Cross-check a Seer's SAME/DIFFERENT results against deaths and Katana holders before trusting them. Carol's comparisons were consistent with Judy's Veteran kill and Alice's Katana holding, and that consistency is what made her credible. Require at least two independent confirmations of a power-role claim before using it to convict.

Alerting on a night you are not attacked burns a token for no information, and a claimed 'bluff alert' is unverifiable. If you claim to have killed someone with alert, say the attacker's role is unknown to you and announce the kill only once it is public, to keep the claim believable.

Plan the endgame around exact vote math. With 2 Yakuza against 2 Village you cannot lose a nomination or trial vote: block with No votes, kill one Village player with the Katana, then nominate and hang the last one at 2 of 3. Pre-agree the continuation in night chat in case a teammate dies mid-plan.

Hang early Day 2 mislynches by joining the town's pile-on with a nomination framed as 'to hear a defense'. Vote Guilty with the majority. Innocent voters get more suspicion later, and our Guilty bloc was never punished for the Frank hang.

A Ritualist with a teammate's Diviner result can guess exact roles with no risk of a public announcement. Use the guaranteed guesses on likely Seer or Eavesdropper claimants, and save Katana shots for power roles.

Stay quiet and keep a consistent Vanilla claim. Don't hint at the Wiretap in public. Town's own 'no PMs because of Wiretap' warning killed all PM evidence, so the real danger was teammates PMing, not you.

Teammates should not PM each other during the Day. Mallory and Bob's PMs were publicly noticed and cited as a tell by Carol. Use night chat only, and never write plans like 'Grace can read this through Wiretap' in a PM.

Do not shoot on Day 1 or Day 2 purely over perceived behavioral slips or awkward questions without mechanical contradictions; shooting an unconfirmed Villager (like Surveyor) accelerates evil's route to parity.
Avoid converting early stacked soft leans and minor timeline slips into Day 2 executions; mislynching a Vanilla Villager immediately concedes momentum and numbers to evil.

When a Ballot Stuffer is active, trial majorities require strictly more than half of all counted votes (including the stuffed vote). If town cannot reach a majority due to parity or stuffed votes, nominations cannot succeed and night actions must be coordinated instead.

Separate a nomination to hear a defense from an execution decision. Before voting Guilty, state what new evidence upgraded your suspicion and why an innocent explanation no longer fits. Several people repeating the same weak concern does not create independent evidence.

Unexpected role-specific questions can come from concealed investigative information. Ask what supports the question before treating it as malicious fishing. Erin's questions about Seer had a Surveyor basis; inaccurate public arguments did not make her a safe Vigilante target.

Distinguish corroborating one entry in an information claim from verifying the entire claim. An extra trial vote proves a Ballot Stuffer exists, not that every role in a claimed archive is authentic. Keep roster deductions conditional until the claimant or additional evidence establishes them.

Recalculate the execution threshold when votes are manipulated. Seven living players with one active Ballot Stuffer produce eight counted trial votes, requiring five Guilty. Comparing revealed votes with totals can also locate the extra vote's side: four revealed Guilty but four counted Guilty puts the stuffer among the Innocent voters.

Choose targets for next-day survival and likely private-message activity, not merely current suspiciousness. You need both yourself and your target alive, plus actual PM traffic, to obtain useful evidence. Track public PM endpoints when available, and never treat silence or an empty interception record as an alignment clear.

Once you publicly claim Veteran, Yakuza will simply avoid you, so later alerts are mostly wasted. Claim only when it confirms a kill or saves a lynch, and do it after you have used your best alerts. If you keep tokens after claiming, don't reveal the count. An honest 'tokens left' tells evil exactly when it is safe to visit you.

When a Ritualist is known to be alive with tokens, every public exact-role claim (Seer, Archivist, Eavesdropper) is close to a guaranteed kill. A living Diviner also feeds the Ritualist exact roles. Delay claims until they change a vote, and count the Ritualist as an extra nightly kill on top of the Katana.

Plan around evil's kill capacity per night (Katana + Ritualist + any Vigilante misfire), not just the head count. At 4 Village vs 3 Yakuza with a Ballot Stuffer that forces 4-4 ties, one lynch-free day plus two evil kills a night is fatal. Kill the stuffer at night first, or find a way to hang before the stuffer's tokens make trials impossible.

An announced trial total that is higher than the number of voters proves a Ballot Stuffer exists. That can mechanically confirm an Archivist or other claim that lists Ballot Stuffer. Use it at once to resolve competing claims, such as which Vigilante claimant is fake.

Telling the confirmed Vigilante publicly whom to shoot also marks the Vigilante for the Katana that night. Once roles are confirmed, write a full will, and accept that the claimed power role dies next.

Calculate defensive uses of your token, not just execution majorities. With three Yakuza against four villagers, one doubled Innocent vote creates eight total trial votes: four Guilty cannot reach the required five. Spend before the critical Day; nomination votes remain unaffected.

Once exposed, prioritize vote control over maintaining appearances. Do not bus a teammate when coordinated Innocent votes can prevent execution. At 2v2, coordinated No votes block nominations requiring three Yes; parity does not itself end this variant.

Plan simultaneous night trades and the surviving team's continuation explicitly. Killing a Vigilante does not cancel their shot. Combining a confirmed Ritualist attack with the Katana can still secure the endgame despite losing a teammate, provided the survivors know exactly whom to kill and how to vote afterward.

Against a revealed Veteran, kill other villagers and execute the Veteran once you have a nomination majority. Do not trust public claims that alert tokens are exhausted: token-history claims can be bait, and hanging bypasses Veteran defenses.

Indirect information can reveal an exact role to a Ritualist. A survey result naming one role among several players may identify the survivor after other members flip. Consider that exposure before requesting public confirmations; private disclosure is also unsafe when a Wiretap may exist.

Never spend a shot on a pure behavioral hunch (I shot Erin, a Surveyor, on a weak read). It cost Village a power role and a token, and Mallory's matching false claim muddied the Vigilante identity. Hold shots until a flipped Yakuza, a mechanical result or a hard contradiction gives a target.

When evil has a Ballot Stuffer or the Day count is distorted, the votes needed shift. Prioritize killing the Katana holder and Ritualist early, and don't spend nominations that can't pass. Plan so the final 4-5 players aren't a tied or minority vote where evil can't be stopped.

If a Yakuza fake-claims your role first and copies your wording and facts, claim immediately with details only the true holder knows (token count, real reasoning). Also record the claim in your will, since a late counterclaim reads as an echo.

Combine mechanical facts: an extra vote total proves a Ballot Stuffer exists, and Archivist counts and flipped roles let you rule out Vanilla slots. Act on such deductions when majority is still reachable, rather than waiting until a 4-4 tie blocks you.

Once the Katana holder is unknown and a Ritualist is alive, assume investigative roles who have publicly claimed with strong info are the next night kills. Spread protection or keep power claims hidden until needed; the Medic was absent and nothing protected our claimed Seer and Archivist.

Don't convert a pile of weak leans into a Guilty vote, especially when the nominator framed it as 'just to hear a defense'. Before voting Guilty, require one claim-based or mechanical contradiction. Count how many Guilty votes come from players whose own reasons were echoes of others.
evidence: Day 2: Grace (Yakuza) nominated Frank 'to hear a defense'. Six players voted Guilty on a corrected timeline slip and his Vanilla claim, Heidi and Judy among them. Frank flipped Vanilla Villager. That one mislynch later let the Ballot Stuffer lock all trials at 4-4.

tip: Don't fire on a soft behavioral read early while Village holds a majority. A misfire costs the same as a mislynch and can hand Yakuza vote parity. Wait for a mechanical lead (a flip, a claim conflict, votes that contradict stated reads) before spending a shot.
evidence: Night 2: Niaj shot Erin (Surveyor) on a 'bad read'. Erin's votes had actually matched her stated lean. With Ivan and Frank also gone, Day 3 started at 4 Village vs 3 Yakuza with a stuffed vote, so no trial could pass.

tip: Never put another living player's power role in your last will or in public when a Ritualist may be alive. A known exact role is a guaranteed, unannounced kill for the Ritualist. Write wills like 'one of X/Y holds info; ask them' and let the role holder decide when to claim.
evidence: Erin's will stated that Carol or Frank was the Seer, which pointed to Carol once Frank flipped Vanilla. Carol then confirmed Seer publicly on Day 3. Bob guessed 'Carol = Seer' with his last token on Night 3 and killed her with no public announcement.

tip: Chain your exact-role checks into Ritualist guesses. A Diviner or Mortician result, or a role claim read by the Wiretap, gives a 100% Ritualist kill that never outs the Ritualist. That frees the Katana for a second kill the same night.
evidence: Alice's Night 1 Diviner check showed Ivan was the Eavesdropper. On Night 2 Bob spent 1 token on 'Ivan = Eavesdropper' and killed him while the Katana went elsewhere. On Night 3 the same pattern took Carol, giving a double kill both nights.

tip: Let the Katana be held by the member whose own role is least valuable, such as the Wiretap or a Grunt. Avoid holders like the Diviner, and avoid sending the Katana into unclaimed vocal organizers, who may be an alerting Veteran.
evidence: Night 2: Alice, the Diviner and the team's exact-role source, held the Katana and attacked Judy. Judy was on Veteran alert and killed her. Grace (Wiretap) had no night action and could have held the Katana instead, keeping the Diviner alive.

tip: As Ballot Stuffer, do the trial math in night chat and spend a token on the night that brings your team close to half. A doubled Innocent vote can block every trial the next Day, even after your teammates are fully exposed.
evidence: Mallory spent a token on Night 2, predicting a 4-of-8 position. On Day 3 Grace was exposed by Heidi's archive, yet her trial ended 4-4 and was ruled Innocent. Town admitted no execution was possible that Day.

tip: Use role-elimination from an exact-role result: the Archivist's list plus flips plus claims can prove which claims are impossible (e.g. no Vanilla slot). Village exact-role holders should still claim the moment they're nominated. The earlier the result is posted, the more it is worth.
evidence: Day 3: Heidi's archive (Ballot Stuffer, Diviner, Ritualist, Surveyor, Veteran, Wiretap) plus the Seer/Eavesdropper/Vigilante slots proved Bob's and Grace's Vanilla claims false. It also exposed Mallory's Vigilante counterclaim. It came only after Heidi was nominated, and the vote math was already lost.

tip: Before fake-claiming a Village power role, check whether its real holder is likely alive and able to counterclaim. An immediate counterclaim plus a mechanical role list exposes you. Prefer to hold a claim when the votes already protect you.
evidence: Day 3: Mallory claimed Vigilante, Niaj instantly counterclaimed, and town shot Mallory that night. The 4-4 vote lock, not the claim, was what actually saved Grace.

tip: A clean token is spent even if the target survives. Clean only when the kill is near-certain (a target with no possible Defense, such as a confirmed Ex-Con), or when the target's will is likely to expose something critical, like a puppeting notice. Never clean a target whose survival is in doubt.

Against a Fortune Teller, put the Katana on the teammate whose own action targets the same player. The kill and the clean (or the divine) then count as a single visitor, which keeps the visit counts consistent with public claims. Plan before each night who holds the Katana and what that does to the visitor and target counts.

Teammates who post near-identical vote justifications back to back look scripted, and town will call it out. Agree on the vote in night chat, but give each person a different argument in different wording. Don't have one teammate open with a one-line nomination and the others echo it.

A Katana attack that fails with no Medic claimed usually means the target has their own Defense: an Arsonist or Serial Killer (Standard), or an Executioner or Jester (Basic). A late Medic claim made only once on trial is suspect. As Yakuza, push such a player to the gallows rather than wasting more night kills on them.

Night deaths are checked together. When one kill wins the game, the Katana holder can visit a possibly trapped or alerted target safely: the team still wins even if the holder dies. Before that point, avoid visiting players likely to be trapped, and rotate the Katana so a trap or Veteran can't take out a key role.

Save the rig for the day your team controls nominations, or for one specific nomination you can steer. Then the target dies even if the town votes Innocent. Expect the rig to be announced whenever the Guilty vote fails, which publicly confirms a Clerk exists. Spend it when the payoff is large, such as removing a strong town player near parity.

The Fortune Teller's second number counts only players who visited someone ELSE, so self-targets don't add to it. Before you build or attack a case on visit counts, check exactly what each number measures. A math error in public gets corrected and costs credibility.
Don't post near-identical vote justifications back to back with a teammate. Town reads matching wording as a night-chat script. Vary your reasons and phrasing, or have one teammate vote silently.

Once your team has a voting majority alone (for example 3 vs 2), stop arguing and just nominate and vote. Hang the most dangerous remaining town role first, such as a possible Veteran, then finish with the night kill. Deaths are checked together, so a trap on the final target can't save town.

Track where a Trapper's trap could be. Every visit that survives rules a player out, and the Trapper's PM partners are the likeliest trap spots. Avoid visiting the likely trapped player until the final winning night, when a trap death no longer matters.

Never hint publicly that your night action 'doesn't visit'. The Yakuza read that as 'possible Veteran' and simply never visit you, which wastes every alert. Claim Vanilla Villager, or better, quietly claim something juicy, such as an investigator, to bait a Katana visit on the night you alert.

Alert on the nights you are most likely to be visited: right after you've drawn attention, defended someone, or made a bait claim. Don't burn tokens on quiet nights. Three empty alerts gave the Village nothing.

When a player flips Yakuza, the people who voted No or argued hardest to save them are the top suspects for the next hang. That ranks above someone who was fooled and then turned on them. Here both No voters on the Diviner were Yakuza, and we hanged the Philanthropist instead.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller visit-count arithmetic when unknown visitors may exist (Arsonist douses, Medic, a second Yakuza action). Those counts have too many free variables to break a claim, and here they led to hanging a real Philanthropist.

A player who switches role claims mid-day under pressure (e.g. 'VV, thanked a Medic', then 'Medic' once on trial) and survived a Katana hit is far more likely a Neutral with Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer) than town. Don't spend credibility defending them. Also, in the endgame the Yakuza vote as a bloc, so count possible Yakuza votes before each day and push hangs while the Village still holds a majority.

On Day 1, don't be the player who steers the discussion or calls out quiet players. The Yakuza often pick the most active, leader-like voice as their first kill. Post generic agreement and save your influence for when you have information.

Write your planned night target into your last will during your Day turn, before the night (e.g. 'N1 plan: block X'). If you die that night, the town still learns who you visited. An empty 'log will be updated' will is wasted if you die on Night 1.

When a Clerk rig is revealed, the Yakuza wanted that nominee dead. Treat the nominator and every Guilty voter on the rigged trial as prime suspects, and hang from that group next. Don't let the conversation drift back to old suspects.

Don't hang on a single Fortune Teller count that has an innocent alternative (e.g. 'the target may have switched', or 'the Katana holder also used their own action'). Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one Yakuza can count as one visitor on two targets. Require a second independent source before a mis-hang can cost parity.

A Diviner who picks a teammate gives them Strong Defense (useful against traps). The 'result' can then be published as a fake survey that clears them, e.g. 'VV shown'. Puppeting a confirmed villager to push a mislynch is very strong, especially when paired with a Clerk rig that same Day.

applies_to: Oracle (and any investigator whose result arrives after the night's kill)
tip: Once you are publicly confirmed, assume you die tonight. Write your will to be conditional and hedged, e.g. 'Tonight I am guessing X = role Y; the result is unknown if I'm dead, so don't hang X on my will alone.' A strong accusation in a will you can no longer update can hang a villager. Here my will's 'Ivan is very suspicious' helped get the real Philanthropist hanged, even though my last guess had confirmed him.

Spend exact-role guesses on the claimed roles of players acting suspiciously, such as 'Alice = Vanilla Villager' or 'Frank = Surveyor'. A WRONG result exposes a liar at once, and a RIGHT result clears them. Confirming a role that was already claimed and is harmless (Ex-Con) gives little and is easy to dismiss as 'anyone could call that'. Test the defenders of a flipped Yakuza, and cheap unverifiable claims like VV, early.

Never hang on a visit-count contradiction that depends on someone's stated 'plan' (a will saying 'N2 plan: audit X'). Players switch targets, and Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. Before hanging a claimed power role on count math, check every combination: who held the Katana, whether the holder also used their own action, and hidden Neutrals such as Arsonist douses.

In the endgame, compare voting blocs, not arguments. Players who voted together on every lynch, and whose Guilty messages repeat the same script, are probably the Yakuza team. The Clerk's rig shows the Yakuza wanted that nominee dead, so look hard at whoever nominated and voted Guilty on that day. Also, count how many Yakuza could still be alive before a vote that can lose the game.

Divining a Yakuza partner gives them Strong Defense (it stops traps and Vigilante shots up to Strong) and still produces a real visit you can publish as a fake 'survey' covering them. Pair it with the Katana holder on risky nights. Town should note that a Diviner/Surveyor 'clearing' a group that later produces a claimer is a classic cover.

applies_to: Diviner (Yakuza) or any Yakuza fake-claiming a token role
tip: A fake token-role claim can be checked by an Accountant (you show 0) and limits how many nights you can report. A Philanthropist's gift to a role with no tokens is thrown away and isn't counted, so 'he gave me a token' does not protect you from an audit. Either report only as many results as the claimed role's tokens allow, or claim a role whose results don't depend on tokens.

If you publish your real Diviner reads as a Surveyor, they come out true far more often than a Roleplayer's would. That kills the 'I must be a Roleplayer' fallback once an Oracle calls WRONG. Mix in at least one harmless false or unconfirmable result early, so a Roleplayer pivot stays believable.

Fortune Teller numbers are unordered. The 'visited someone else' number excludes self-targets, and a Katana holder using their own action is one visitor on two targets. Before you build a case on equal or unequal numbers, list every way they could fit: a holder acting twice, self-protects, hidden Neutral douses, Ex-Con random visits.

Hold the Clerk rig and the Puppeteer token for the turn where the Yakuza vote bloc is close to half. Then any nomination your bloc can pass is a guaranteed execution, which can turn 3v4 into a won game. Once you have a voting majority, stop arguing and just vote as a bloc.

On the winning night, the Katana holder may walk into a trap freely, because all of the night's deaths are checked together. Earlier in the game, have the Diviner pick the holder to give Strong Defense against a suspected trap, or attack the Trapper herself, who can't trap her own player.

Audit the newest claimed token role, such as Surveyor, Philanthropist or Medic, early. Yakuza fake-claim token roles to explain Diviner-style results, and a 0-token count on a claimed Surveyor exposes a Diviner. Work out the expected count before you audit, including spent tokens and any Philanthropist gifts, so you can act on the result right away.

Never announce publicly which player or claim you will check tonight. If you die that night, the result dies with you, because your will can't be updated. Announcing it just tells the Yakuza whom to kill first. Avoid visible PM exchanges with claimers for the same reason.

When a player flips Yakuza, look hardest at who voted No on their nomination or argued to delay the hang. Don't follow the flipped player's own allies' deflections onto confirmed-consistent claimers. Players who defended the Yakuza and then smoothly joined the next push are prime suspects.

In the endgame, count the worst case. If every unconfirmed Guilty voter could be Yakuza, don't hang on a thin case: a mis-hang at 5 alive can hand the Yakuza the win. Also remember a Clerk rig executes anyone nominated, so be careful about which nominations you let pass on a day that may be rigged.

A Diviner's reads are true about 60% of the time, so accurate results that match later flips do not clear a self-claimed Surveyor. Look for checks the fake can't survive: token audits, exact-role guesses, and visit counts that conflict with gift or visit claims.

Ignite as soon as 3 or more living players are doused, or as soon as you come under any suspicion. Each night spent dousing is a night the town can hang you first. Ignite is an Astral Visit, so it is trap-safe and adds nothing to Fortune Teller counts. A mass kill also thins the field and can wipe out a whole Evil team. Waiting until 'the right moment' let me get hanged with three doused players still alive.

applies_to: Serial Killer, Arsonist, any role with innate Defense
tip: If you survive a night attack, nobody else knows who the target was. When asked, deny being attacked. Admitting survival as a claimed Vanilla Villager points straight at innate Defense. If you must explain it, pick one consistent claim right away (e.g. Medic who self-protected). Never say 'thanks, Medic' and then switch claims later.

A Fortune Teller's 'hidden visitor every night' that no town role claims is often a Neutral killer dousing or attacking. Neutrals should expect visit counts to expose them over time. Town should treat any player with no claimed night action who stays unaccounted for as a candidate.

Watch for players who vote together on every key hang, defended a flipped Yakuza, and later lead pushes on proven town investigators. They are likely the Evil team. Douse or kill them first: removing the Yakuza leaves a smaller town that you can outlast. Dousing likely Yakuza also means one ignite can hit them all.

Once a Clerk rig is possible (an unused Clerk token, or a Yakuza count near half), any passed nomination may be lethal. If you are a likely target, vote No at the nomination stage, because the trial vote may not save you.

A group-check result (Surveyor/Diviner style: group of 3 plus one role) that matches your own true role does not verify the checker. A Yakuza Diviner gets the true role 60% of the time, and the same output also matches a Surveyor. Before vouching for a group-check claimer, require an independent check such as an Oracle guess, an Accountant token audit or a visit count.

Only give tokens to someone whose role has been verified by something other than their own claim. Never announce publicly whom you plan to gift: a fake token-role claimer can then build the gift into their story. You are never told whether the token was thrown away, so a gift proves nothing about the recipient. It also ties your credibility to theirs if they flip Yakuza.

applies_to: everyone (especially when Fortune Teller counts are used against you)
tip: FT numbers count visitors and visited players separately. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action is one visitor on two targets. Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) therefore do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. A double visit on one target can be offset by one visitor hitting two targets. Run this counter-scenario out loud before accepting 'the count has no room for your visit'.

On trial, lead with one concrete, checkable alternative explanation of the evidence (spell out the exact visit assignment that fits the numbers), not a counter-accusation. Pointing at the accuser reads as deflection, while a worked example that makes the case collapse can actually move votes.

Track who voted No or argued to save a player who later flips Yakuza (here Olivia and Alice), and who quietly piggybacks short scripted Guilty lines. Keep pushing those reads even after you've been wrong once. Defenders of a flipped Yakuza are the highest-value suspects going into the endgame.

Equal numbers (e.g. 6&6) do NOT prove nobody was double-visited. One visitor can hit two targets: a Katana holder who also uses their own role's action counts once as a visitor but adds two visited players. That offsets a double-visit elsewhere. Self-targeting actions also change the second number. Before using a count to accuse, list every possible way it could fit.

Don't lead a hang on one unverifiable inference from your own results, especially when the target has a coherent, checkable claim. A mis-hang costs the hanged villager and also your own credibility, which the Yakuza will then use against you. Prefer targets backed by flips or vote records.

When a player flips Yakuza, the players who voted No or argued hardest to save them become your top suspects the next Day. Only claimed-Vanilla players defending a confirmed Yakuza are especially suspect. Act on that before chasing the people who vouched for the dead Yakuza's fake results; those people may simply have been fooled.

Estimate Yakuza size early: in ~13-player games expect about 4. Track blocs that vote identically on every contested trial. Three players always voting together on narrow votes, plus near-identical justifications, is a strong team tell. Push to hang one of them while Village still holds the majority, not when it's too late.

A Diviner who picks a Yakuza partner gets no result, so any 'survey' they publish about that group is invented. A teammate claiming the role the fake result reported, right after it appears, is suspicious. Cross-check every survey-style claim against whether its source could have fabricated it.

Never narrow down your trap's location in public or in private messages, e.g. 'not on X, Y, Z'. A private-message exchange with one player also hints the trap is on them. The Yakuza use every exclusion to route their kills around the trap. A Trapper can't trap themself, so once you are identified you are a free, safe kill. Let your role be identified as late as possible, and keep the trap's mere existence as a deterrent to everyone.

An investigator whose 'results' only ever confirm roles that were already claimed or publicly deduced, such as Philanthropist or Trapper, is not verified. That pattern is exactly what a Yakuza Diviner, or a fake claimer, produces. Only trust group or role results that revealed something nobody had said yet, or that a token or visit count independently confirms.

Don't vouch for other players in your last will unless something independent of their own claims has verified them. When you die, your endorsement gets extra weight. If that player is Yakuza, your will props them up and makes the town hesitate.

If a Clerk might still hold a token, a passed nomination may mean execution no matter how the trial vote goes. In the late game, treat your Yes on a nomination as if it were a Guilty vote. Don't vote Yes on someone you'd want to hear defend themselves first.

Look for small blocs that voted together on every mis-hang, both pushing the case and voting Guilty. Repeated identical votes plus near-identical wording is a strong team signal. In this game the three Yakuza voted as a bloc on every trial from Day 5 on. Cross-check vote patterns every day rather than only at the end.

When a Yakuza investigator flips, go back over every result they published. Anyone they 'cleared' (for example 'group X shows Vanilla Villager') is suspect, because a Diviner who picks a partner gets no read and can invent the result. On the other hand, their reads on non-partners were often true, so don't hang someone like a Philanthropist just because the flipped Yakuza 'confirmed' them.

Don't hang on Fortune Teller arithmetic alone. Hidden actors (Arsonist douses, Medics, Ex-Con visits, a Katana holder using two actions, 'plan' wills) can make almost any count fit. Treat a count that breaks as weak evidence, never as enough for a hang, especially against a claim backed by an exact-role or flip result.

Players who voted No on the nomination of someone who then flips Yakuza, and argued for that player in the trial, should be your top suspects for the rest of the game. Push them before ambiguous suspects. At 7 or fewer players, three coordinated Yakuza votes decide everything, so find them while town still holds the majority.

applies_to: Village (any role that can be puppeted)
tip: If you're told you are puppeted, write it in your last will at once, because the Yakuza will likely kill you that night. The player who immediately backs your puppet's accusation (here, whoever nominated right after 'my' push) is very likely the Puppeteer; say so in the will. Your votes are still your own, so vote by your own reads, not by what the puppet said.

Once a Clerk might have an unused token, any nomination that passes that Day can mean an execution no matter how the trial goes. Vote Yes on a nomination only if you'd accept that player dying. Note who on the Guilty side wanted the rigged hang, because they're likely the Clerk's team.

When a teammate's nomination is clearly going to pass, don't be one of the few No votes. Voting No marks you as a defender, and town used that No-vote list for the rest of the game. Bus quietly, or cast one soft dissent without arguing hard.

Puppet the most trusted confirmed villager (for example, an Oracle-confirmed role) on the day you need a swing vote. Their public word moves the undecided players. Pair it with a Clerk rig so any nomination you push gets executed. Kill the puppeted player that night, before they can out the puppeting the next day.

If a Katana hit fails and nobody credibly claims Medic, the survivor most likely has their own Defense (Arsonist or Serial Killer). Push to hang them: it removes a third-party threat, and it looks pro-town in later days.

Plan visits around the Fortune Teller's counts. A Katana holder who also uses their own role action counts as one visitor. Explaining every night's visitors with claimed actions keeps the counts clean. Mismatched counts give town 'hidden visitor' evidence.

A Trapper's trap stays after the Trapper dies. Track which players were visited without anyone dying, since that rules those players out as the trap's location. For a risky final kill, let the teammate with the least useful remaining role hold the Katana. Deaths are checked together, so a killing blow still wins even if the trap kills the holder.

applies_to: Fortune Teller and everyone using visit counts
tip: One player can visit two targets in one night, most often a Katana holder who also uses their own role action. So equal FT numbers do NOT prove that nobody was visited twice. Before using a count to call someone a liar, list every case where one visitor covers several targets.
evidence: N2 gave 6&6 because Frank held the Katana: he attacked Grace and also divined Mallory. That left room for both Grace and Ivan to visit Frank. Judy read 6&6 as 'no double visits', concluded Ivan's token visit was fake, and led the hang of Ivan, a villager.

tip: After a Yakuza flips, look first at the players who voted No on their nomination or argued hardest to delay the hang. Voting Guilty once the trial is clearly lost is cheap cover. Do not jump to a new theory built on a disputed count instead.
evidence: Only Alice and Olivia voted No on Frank's nomination. Olivia defended him at length, and both then voted Guilty. Ivan pointed this out on D5, but town hanged Ivan anyway. Alice and Olivia were both Yakuza.

tip: Spend Oracle guesses on players' public role claims. A RIGHT confirms the claimer, and a WRONG on a trusted investigator's claim exposes a fake whose results only seemed to check out.
evidence: Erin guessed Frank = Surveyor (his public claim) and got WRONG. That broke a cover Ivan, Grace's audit plan and two 'matching' flips had all appeared to support, and Frank was hanged and flipped Diviner. Her earlier RIGHT on Niaj = Ex-Con had confirmed a villager.

tip: Keep track of who you have doused and who is still alive. Ignite once several living players are doused and you are under day pressure, before a hang or a kill can remove you. A douse that is never ignited does nothing.
evidence: By N5 Heidi had doused Olivia, Bob and Alice, all three living Yakuza. Igniting that night would have killed all three. She doused again instead, was exposed by surviving the Katana, and was hanged on D6.

tip: Claim a role whose results look like yours, such as Surveyor for a Diviner. At night, choose the Katana holder so the visits match what your team has claimed, and divine a teammate who must visit a possibly trapped player, which gives them Strong Defense. If a teammate's hang is certain, vote for it to protect your own credibility.
evidence: Frank's 'Surveyor' results fooled town for three days. The team picked holders deliberately so Judy's counts matched their stories. On N3 Frank divined Bob, the holder, for Strong Defense. Bob voted Yes and Guilty on Frank and stayed unsuspected until the very end.

tip: Save one-shot tokens for a single decisive endgame day, and use them together. Rig the votes so any nomination that passes kills. Puppet a trusted villager to push the hang. Clean the puppeted player when you kill them, so their will cannot reveal the puppeting.
evidence: On N5 Bob rigged Day 6 and Olivia puppeted Niaj, the confirmed town player. Heidi was executed despite a 4-3 Innocent vote. Alice then killed and cleaned Niaj, which hid his will saying he had been puppeted. That left 3v2, and the Yakuza won.

tip: Do not announce publicly which claimed role you plan to give a token to. The Philanthropist never learns whether the token was used, and a fake claimer can simply 'confirm' receiving it. Give tokens only after a claim has been checked independently.
evidence: On Day 2 Ivan announced he would give Frank a survey token. On D3 Frank 'confirmed' it, and the two vouched for each other. Frank was a Diviner who threw the token away. When Frank was exposed, Ivan looked like his partner and was hanged.

applies_to: Veteran and other hidden power roles
tip: Do not say that your night action 'doesn't visit'. That points straight at Veteran (or Oracle), and the Yakuza will just avoid you. Stay vague or claim a role with no action, so that your alerts can actually catch a visitor.
evidence: Carol said her action doesn't visit, and the Yakuza chat repeatedly said 'avoid Carol (possible Veteran)'. She alerted on N3, N4 and N6 and caught no one, then was hanged at 5 alive with 0 tokens.

tip: When an Archivist/role list is public, do slot math right away: count listed roles plus unseen slots against the living players. Two players claiming the same listed role means one is Evil. A claim that pushes the unseen slots over their count is the cheapest lie to catch. A quiet 'Vanilla' sitting in an unseen slot deserves a test too.

Once a counterclaim proves someone false (e.g. a second Vigilante claim against a list showing one), shoot them that night with enough Attack to beat Standard Defense. Don't wait. Expect to be Katana'd right after counterclaiming, so make sure your shot is already queued.

If an announced trial total doesn't match the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists. Compare whose side the extra vote helped against who has unverified claims. A self-described 'no-action' role (Vanilla, or a Roleplayer hidden behind fake results) is the natural cover for a Ballot Stuffer or Wiretap.

Fake-claiming a role that appears on a public role list is very risky: the real holder will counterclaim and both flips get compared. Prefer roles outside the list and fake results that can't be checked. Don't openly defend a teammate who is about to be hanged, because voting patterns get reviewed after every flip.

Keep your last will updated with your claim and planned action every turn. A dead townie's will that names the liars, as Alice's and Dave's did, carries the town's logic even after the Katana kills them.

Don't write a last will that both fake-claims a Village role and accuses your target. Your role is revealed on death, so the will instantly reads as Executioner noise and actually clears your target. Use a will that says nothing about the target, or a short truthful one.

Avoid being the loudest or sharpest voice on Day 1. Yakuza often kill whoever sounds like a protective or info role. Blend in until you have a real chance to push your target, because you can only win while alive.

Don't attack your target directly early on. Instead, quietly support any legitimate case or wagon that forms against them and vote Guilty. A visible personal vendetta against one player is the classic Executioner tell.

When an Archivist or full role list appears, do the slot math: count the listed roles alive against the claims. Duplicate claims on listed roles, and unseen-slot overflows, expose liars quickly. A player who sits on a soft claim like Vanilla in an unseen slot is the last suspect standing at the endgame.
A late counterclaim, made only when prosecuted or nominated, is almost never believed. If you plan to claim a 'results are fake' slot like Roleplayer, claim it early, before a townie takes it.

Don't open by teasing 'I have role info, claim to me' without revealing anything; it looks scummy and forces a claim anyway. Either post the anonymous list right away, or post the list without naming your role. A named Archivist claim is a guaranteed Ritualist hit.

An Archivist list turns the game into slot math: alive players = listed roles minus flips, plus N unseen slots. Count claims against those slots every day. Overflowing the unseen slots or duplicating a listed role exposes a liar, and the last unverified unseen-slot claim is usually Yakuza.

applies_to: Village info roles with exact-role results
tip: Any role that publicly claims a unique, confirmable role (Archivist, Seer, Prosecutor) should expect a near-certain Ritualist kill that night. Put everything useful in your last will before claiming, so your death still delivers the info.

Watch announced trial totals against the revealed votes. A mismatch reveals a Ballot Stuffer exists, and doubled Innocents point at the Innocent voters. Also, a player who later claims Roleplayer but stayed silent while others claimed that slot is very likely lying.

Delay-the-hang pitches ('the test settles it tomorrow, Innocent costs nothing') are a classic Yakuza line. If the flip resolves several linked claims at once, hang today rather than give the Katana a free night.

When an Archivist list is public, do strict slot math every day: alive players = remaining listed roles + unseen slots. Each unverified claim on an unseen slot (e.g. 'Vanilla') is the prime hiding spot for a hidden Yakuza like a Ballot Stuffer or Grunt. Press those claims early, not last.

A random-pair 'SAME' result only links two players. Once one of them flips or is proven, chain it right away. Remember the Katana-holder exception (reads Good) before calling anyone cleared. Spend the chosen-pair token on a known-alignment player plus a suspect so the result is a clean read.

Watch who argues Innocent or 'wait a day' on contested hangs, even if they flip to Guilty at the end. Several players pushing the same 'coin flip, wait for tomorrow' line usually includes Yakuza protecting a teammate.

A fake Roleplayer claim only works if it's posted before the real Roleplayer claims and before the info it 'contradicts' is public. Fake results made up after the deaths, especially ones landing on the night's victims, get spotted easily.

Once you've claimed publicly, expect a Ritualist guess or the Katana that night. Put every result and your full reasoning in your last will before the night ends, so your info still helps the Village after you die.

applies_to: Yakuza (any role without a checkable action)
tip: Choose your fake claim with the end-game role math in mind. When an Archivist list is public, an unseen-slot claim like Vanilla becomes the last unverified slot once the other claims are confirmed. Early on, pick a claim that can survive elimination, such as a listed role whose real holder is likely dead, or a slot you can contest later. Never switch claims only once you're cornered.

Don't vote No or Innocent alongside teammates on a wagon you're going to lose anyway. Bloc voting with flipped Yakuza is the first thing town uses to find the next one. If a teammate's hang is clearly happening, bus them early and visibly, on the nomination too, not just the trial.

If you plan to counterclaim a slot like Roleplayer later, do it the moment the slot is contested (e.g. when two others claim it). Claiming it only after you're prosecuted reads as a desperation grab and is easily refuted with 'you would have known both were lying earlier'.

A doubled vote shows up as a mismatch in the trial totals and confirms a Ballot Stuffer exists. That narrows the role math for town. Save it for a day when it actually swings a trial, e.g. lock a no-hang at near-parity. Don't spend it on a day where it doesn't change the outcome.

Kill the Prosecutor (or any role whose result outlasts its user) before they can act on you, or accept that R21 means the effect still happens. Prioritize kills that remove town's confirmation tools early, rather than kills that only thin out numbers.

When an Archivist publishes a role list, fake-claim only unseen roles, and check how many unseen slots are left before claiming. If teammates' claims overflow the slots, the role math corners the whole team. Agree on night chat which teammate takes which unseen or listed slot, so nobody double-claims (e.g. two Roleplayers, two Vigilantes).

Don't all vote No/Innocent together on a teammate's trial when it's clearly lost. A same-alignment Seer pair or a counterclaim already links you, and a bloc vote ties every defender to the flip. Bus the doomed teammate, or let only one of you defend.

applies_to: Yakuza (Fabricator and anyone writing a will)
tip: Never confess team actions in a last will (e.g. 'I framed X'). It hands town verification that confirms their reads and clears townies. Write a will that keeps your fake claim or sows doubt about a specific townie.

Before using a Ritualist or Katana kill on a confirmed info role, weigh what its flip tells town. A dead Seer or Archivist with a true will can lock in town's deductions. Sometimes it's better to kill the swing voter or the most persuasive reasoner instead.

Count roles exactly: alive players = remaining listed roles + unseen slots. Each confirmed flip or prosecution removes a slot, so endgames often reduce to one unverified claim. Plan your claim so it survives that count.

Once an Archivist list is public, keep a running slot count: alive players = remaining listed roles + unseen slots. Every flip and claim shrinks it, and late game the one unverified 'unseen' claim (often a Vanilla) is usually the hidden Yakuza.
Compare announced trial totals with the revealed votes. An extra counted vote proves a Ballot Stuffer is alive and used a token, which narrows the remaining Yakuza to unverified, actionless claims.

Test a Roleplayer counterclaim against what that player would have known. A real Roleplayer knows every other Roleplayer claim is false, so they would have pushed hard against the fake one. Someone who instead defended the fake claimant is almost certainly Yakuza.
When a blind investigator 'happened' to target exactly the night-kill victims, call it out. Results invented after the deaths cluster on public victims, and this argument swings trial votes.

Eavesdrop on the player most likely to send or receive PMs the next Day, such as the prosecuted player or a swing voter. Never pick someone likely to die that night, since the eavesdrop is wasted if they die.

When an Archivist list is public, do role-slot math: alive players = remaining listed roles + unseen slots. Count the claims that fall outside the list against the number of unseen slots. Any overflow means a liar, and duplicate claims to one listed role mean one of them is lying. This math pinned every Yakuza in this game.

A Prosecutor claim is self-proving, because the prosecution is announced the next Day and Yakuza can't fake it. When you're counterclaimed, offer to prosecute your accuser. Keep the token plan public so that a prosecution still fires and confirms you even if you die that night (R21).

Compare announced trial totals with the revealed votes. A gap means a Ballot Stuffer cast a doubled vote and is still alive. Combine that with the slot math to find which unverified claim (often a 'Vanilla Villager') is the Stuffer.

Track who votes No/Innocent on players who later flip Yakuza, and who steers the hang toward someone who flips town. Yakuza often defend teammates in a coordinated way (the same 'wait for tomorrow's test' pitch from several players). Name that bloc publicly to swing the undecided voters.

A fake claim to an unseen slot (Vanilla, Sheriff) collapses once a public role list and the flips fill in the other slots. Prefer claiming a listed role whose holder is dead or silent, or claim early, before the slot math tightens.

Before fake-claiming a role, check it against any public role list such as an Archivist's. If the list shows exactly one copy of a role that a live townie can hold, that townie will counterclaim. Prefer an unseen slot or a role whose holder is already dead. A collision with a confirmed-unique role is close to an auto-loss for you, and a Seer pair can then chain it onto a teammate.

Once an Archivist list is public, do slot math every day: alive players equal the remaining listed roles plus the unseen slots. Count the claims against the slots. Whoever overflows them, or duplicates a single listed role, is the liar. Town in this game solved every Yakuza this way, so as Evil, plan your claims around the math from Day 2.

Don't have every teammate vote No or Innocent together on a doomed teammate. The vote reveal becomes a public map of the whole team. When a hang is clearly going to land, bus your teammate with Guilty votes and keep the others clean for later days.

Spend Ritualist tokens early on confirmed-role claims, like Archivist or a Seer pinned by a Surveyor group. It gives you a near-certain second kill each night. But keep in mind that every Ritualist kill confirms that both a Ritualist and the dead player's role exist, which tightens town's role math.

If you'll need a fake claim later, settle on one with your team early and keep it consistent. Switching claims late, for example from Vanilla to Roleplayer once prosecuted, is read as a desperate slot grab. Grab any 'my results are fake' slot like Roleplayer early, before a real townie does.

applies_to: Village investigators (especially anyone who might be a Roleplayer)
tip: If your results contradict a flipped role or a confirmed claim, say so publicly and early, before others claim. Volunteering that your own results may be fake reads strongly town. It also locks in a timeline that later fake counterclaimers can't match.

Once an Archivist list exists, keep a running role-slot ledger: listed roles still alive, plus the count of unseen slots. Every death or proven claim shrinks it. In the endgame the last Yakuza is usually whoever sits in the one unverified unseen slot, often a 'Vanilla' claim.

Compare announced vote totals with the revealed votes. A mismatch proves a Ballot Stuffer (or a similar role) is alive and voted that way. Combine that with a night kill after a Yakuza hang to prove a Yakuza is still among the living.

Separate 'wait for a free test' arguments that resolve the actual dispute from ones that don't. Yakuza will co-opt a town player's earlier no-hang plan to save a teammate on an unrelated question. Explicitly say which conflict your plan was for.

A late Roleplayer counterclaim fails if you earlier claimed something else, or voted to protect someone a real Roleplayer would have known was lying. Pick a cover early that survives role-slot math, and don't defend teammates whose claims your cover role would expose.

Once an Archivist-style role list is public, do slot math every Day. Count the living listed roles against the unseen slots, then match every claim to a slot. A claim that overflows the unseen slots or duplicates a listed role marks the liar. Late-game, the Yakuza usually hides in the one unseen slot that nobody's results have verified, often a 'Vanilla' claim.

Always compare an announced vote total with the revealed votes. A mismatch means a Ballot Stuffer (or similar) is alive and voted the way the extra vote went. That narrows the remaining Yakuza to the living players who cast that vote, and it survives even when the Stuffer votes with town for cover.

Judge a Roleplayer counterclaim by when it was made. A real Roleplayer flags their own clashing results early, before others claim. A Yakuza claims the fake-results slot only once cornered or prosecuted. Also ask whether their Day votes match what they would have known: a real Roleplayer knows any other Roleplayer claimant is lying.

Group-based exact-role results become decisive once other claims and flips eliminate group members. Survey a player with plausible but unconfirmed neighbors. Post the full group plus role publicly once claims start, because one dead or flipped neighbor can turn a 1-in-3 into a 1-in-2.

In the late game, hang on the strongest current read rather than accepting 'acquit and test tomorrow' offers. Those offers mostly buy the Yakuza another night kill. A prosecution or flip that is already scheduled resolves things anyway. Watch who pushes Innocent on the same suspect, since they often turn out to be Yakuza teammates.

applies_to: Yakuza (any role faking a 'my results are fake' claim)
tip: If you fake-claim Roleplayer or any investigator, choose your fake targets before the night's deaths could plausibly shape them. Never 'watch' or 'track' exactly the players who died. Also post the fake results on the first day you claim anything. A late claim whose targets line up with the kills reads as invented after the fact.

Once an Archivist list is public, run the town's role-slot math yourself before claiming. Count the listed roles still alive plus the unseen slots, then pick a claim that doesn't overflow the slots or duplicate a slot already credibly taken. If no safe slot exists, claim early as a common unseen role such as Vanilla, before the math corners you.

Don't have several teammates all vote No/Innocent on the same accused teammate and all argue 'wait for tomorrow'. Matching vote blocs become the main evidence in later days. Bus or split votes, and only defend when your votes can actually swing the trial.

Spend Ritualist kills on confirmed claims (Archivist, Seer) early. But first kill the information roles whose results link teammates together, such as a Seer whose random pairs can tie two Yakuza, before those results go public. A Seer pair linking two of you can bring down both if either one is exposed.

Private messages are visible as sent, and the recipient can paste them publicly. Mid-trial lobbying by PM almost always gets exposed and reads as scummy. Make your argument publicly instead, unless the content is truly something you need hidden.

applies_to: Village investigative roles (Tracker, Lookout, Sheriff, etc.)
tip: Never say anything that hints you hold info (e.g. 'I'll hold my info'). The Yakuza picked their kill from exactly that line. Sound like a vanilla townie until you are ready to share a full result.

Track the players most likely to hold the Katana or act at night. Pick people who visibly steer discussion or defend suspects, not passive echoers. A 'did not visit anyone' result on a quiet player wastes the night. The Katana often moves between nights, so a non-visit doesn't clear someone as Yakuza.

When an Archivist list is published, do the slot math right away. Claimed roles must fit into listed roles plus a fixed number of unseen slots. Count overflow and duplicates; a claim like 'Vanilla' sitting in an unseen slot is the easiest place for a Yakuza with no checkable action (Ballot Stuffer, Grunt) to hide.

Watch who votes No/Innocent on a player who later flips Yakuza. Also watch who steers the hang toward a counterclaimant who later flips town. In this format the Yakuza almost always defend teammates at trial, and those vote records later expose them.
Keep your last will updated with every result from the first night, so your info survives if you are killed before claiming. Log each night's result as soon as you get it.

Once an Archivist-style role list is public, agree on fake claims before Day as a team. Each fake must fit an unseen slot that nobody else is likely to claim. Never fake-claim a role the list shows only once, and count how many unseen slots are left so your team's claims don't overflow them.
evidence: Ivan claimed Vigilante, which appeared once on Carol's list, and Alice counterclaimed at once. Frank's Sheriff plus Erin's Vanilla, alongside the real Seer and Prosecutor, made four claims for three unseen slots. Heidi and Mallory used that count to pin the liars.

tip: For the Ritualist: any claim that has been confirmed is a guess that cannot miss, so save your tokens for those claims. For the Village: if a Ritualist is known to exist, a confirmed claim is effectively a death warrant. Put all your information in your will and in public the same day you claim, and don't confirm other players' exact roles casually.
evidence: Carol's list confirmed her as Archivist, and Ivan killed her with a correct guess on Night 2. Mallory's survey located the Seer in Carol/Dave/Erin, Dave claimed Seer, and Ivan killed him on Night 3. Both deaths came from certain guesses.

tip: Fake results must look like you posted them before you knew the outcomes. Don't make them land on the night's victims, and don't fit them around claims other people have just made. A believable fake comes early and says something useful or wrong, not something tidy after the fact.
evidence: Niaj's 'Roleplayer told Lookout' results watched exactly the two Katana victims and were posted after Grace and Dave had claimed. Grace called the odds of that tiny. Dave pointed out that a Roleplayer who believed 'Grace visited Bob' would have shouted it on Day 2.

tip: Don't vote as a bloc to save a teammate who is likely to flip Evil. Spread your votes, or vote against the teammate (bus them) in both the nomination and the trial. Every vote is revealed, and the Village will tie the Innocent voters to each other after the flip.
