evidence: Frank, Ivan, Niaj and Erin all voted No on the Niaj nomination, and Frank and Ivan also voted Innocent. Once Niaj flipped Fabricator, Heidi and Mallory used those votes against Frank on Day 4 and against Erin on Day 5.

applies_to: everyone, especially players who may be the Roleplayer
tip: If your results clash with a flip or with confirmed information, say so first and early. Volunteering that your own results may be fake earns lasting trust. Holding back and counterclaiming only when you are cornered looks like a Yakuza grabbing a free slot.
evidence: Judy said she might be the Roleplayer in her first message on Day 3, before anyone else claimed, and the Village trusted her all game. Niaj claimed Roleplayer only after Mallory's role math cornered him, and was hanged. Erin claimed Roleplayer only after she was prosecuted, and was hanged.

tip: Offer tests that the other side cannot fake, such as a prosecution, a flip or a future check. But don't let a test planned for one conflict stall today's hang on a different conflict. Hang the strongest case today and let the test settle the other one tomorrow.
evidence: Heidi offered her prosecution as proof against Frank, which the Yakuza could not fake. The Yakuza tried to use 'wait for the test' to save Niaj. Grace and Heidi pointed out that the test said nothing about Niaj vs Judy, so they hanged Niaj on Day 3 and Frank on Day 4.

tip: When someone counterclaims your unique role, shoot them that night. The shot is close to certain to hit Evil. It also forces the Yakuza to plan around a death, which can wreck their schemes for the following Day.
evidence: Alice shot Ivan, the false Vigilante, on Night 3. Erin's plan was a doubled Innocent vote with three Yakuza alive so that no trial could pass, and Ivan's death broke it. Erin then had to vote Guilty on Frank.

tip: On early Days, don't signal that you have hidden information or are shielding information roles. Phrases like 'I'll hold my info' or protective meta-arguments make you the obvious Katana target. Blend in until you have something you can act on.
evidence: Olivia said 'I'll hold my info for now' on Day 2, and the Yakuza named that line as their reason for killing her that night. Bob's Day 1 push to shield information roles got him chosen as the Night 1 target.

tip: Use the Oracle's exact-role guess early on a claimed Sheriff or Lookout to verify their role, but remember a Yakuza can also be targeted by Katana for guessing; consider guessing on the most suspicious claimant rather than a claim that is already backed by consistent results.

Before voting on a claim, check whether any result can actually test it; visit lists, private chats and self-nominations alone rarely justify a hanging, and a Guilty vote on an untestable claim should be weighed against losing a live result source.

Track private message counts between players early; repeated private contact between two players who later both prove Yakuza is a strong signal, and it is worth asking both directly what was discussed before the first trial.

Avoid pairing a flat denial with a visit that a Lookout has already recorded; admitting a visit that is provably true while framing it as a benign action is far more credible than denying it outright.

Do not let a self-nomination or early hanging happen on the first Day without any result; a stall on Day 1 that stays unresolved gives Yakuza time to build a story, so push for a quick, checkable result instead.

applies_to: Lookout, Sheriff, Seer and other investigators
tip: Visit lists only show who visited a target, not what they did. Before voting on a visit list, check whether the visitor could be a harmless non-blocker. Investigators should consider posting results early and asking for a second confirmation, rather than letting a single list decide an execution.

Don't let a single unverified claim or self-nomination drive early hangings. Early on, Village players should hold off on executions until at least two independent checkable results exist, since a hanging of a real Village player removes information forever.

Private messages are visible as sent-to events. Yakuza who keep PMing the same Village player during trials create a visible pattern; spread contact out, and avoid pushing 'Innocent' votes via PMs right after your own nomination.

Track who pushes nominations or votes without evidence and who repeatedly PMs the same player. Those patterns were the clearest tell in this game and were easy to miss when everyone was talking at once.

Role-blocks and Medic protections both fail silently, so a dead Village player's claim that protection held is only as good as the Medic's own report. Compare Katana outcomes against protection claims before trusting a Medic.

applies_to: Sheriff, Lookout, Tracker, Seer and other investigators
tip: Post your result as soon as you have it. Delaying to 'the start of the next Day' let Frank and others frame the stall as Yakuza behavior and cost me trust before I had a single result. If a check is blocked, say so immediately and keep the story simple.

A visit list (Lookout, Tracker) proves contact, not role or intent. A blocker must visit, but a visitor is not automatically a blocker. Do not execute on visit lists alone; demand an alignment or exact-role result, or a result that can be tested on a later night.

Watch for players who repeatedly ask others to vote Innocent or to wait for a result that never comes. Asking for checkable evidence is good, but pairing it with private pleas to the same people is a pattern worth tracking, and stalling is often a Yakuza tool.

Private message counts are public. Heavy PM traffic between two players, especially right before or during trials, identifies a pair even when the contents stay hidden. Keep teammate contact minimal and avoid trial-time bursts.

Claiming a protection role late, right after your visit is exposed, looks like a cover story. Claim early when the claim can be checked, and avoid protections that the Village can disprove with a single Katana death.

applies_to: Village roles, especially Lookout and Sheriff
tip: Visit lists from a Lookout are real evidence, not noise. A blocked Sheriff or Medic must have a visitor, so cross-check the Lookout's visitor list against the claimed protector or blocker and test which claim fits. Don't dismiss a checkable visit result as just a visit list.

Count the win conditions of neutral roles when few players remain. With 11 starting players, the Vulture wins alone at the start of a Day with max(floor(N/4),2)=2 alive, and a Jester wins by being hanged. Before any hanging with 3 or 4 players left, check whether the hanged player's win condition benefits from it.

When a player forces a self-nomination or nominates on thin grounds, ask for their role and night action before voting. Don't just vote Guilty to test them, since a Jester or Vulture may want exactly that outcome. Require a checkable result before any hanging.

Track private message counts by pair during every Day, not just who said what publicly. Two players who PM each other heavily during trials and then push the same Innocent votes are a strong Yakuza signal, and the pattern should be weighed as evidence.

Claim protections publicly as soon as they are made, not after a conflicting visit appears. A late Medic claim that explains a visit after exposure looks self-serving and is hard for the table to trust, while an early claim lets the table verify it against kill results.
Keep private-message contact with a teammate minimal and never after a nomination; Judy and Grace's PM networks were exposed by the Day 4 and Day 5 chat logs and made them the obvious pair.

Track role-block and protection results by night: a blocked Medic's protection is void, so a Katana kill on a claimed-protected target points to a Pharmacist-style block, and the Lookout's visitor list is the only way to find the blocker.
Be wary of players who repeatedly push others to vote Innocent on untestable grounds; asking for checkable results is good, but pressuring votes without offering any result is itself a signal.
When a Divine Attack or revenge effect is pending, weigh the cost of your own death before nominating; a nomination that risks your own hanging can hand the Yakuza a free kill.
Check which night actions are visits: role-blocked actions and Astral Visits do not show on a Lookout, so an empty watch does not prove nobody acted on the target.

Jester wins only by being hanged, so a self-nomination with a weak case is the fastest route to a win; push a Village-looking read hard enough that others vote Guilty, and avoid appearing to deliberately get hanged so the vote doesn't look coordinated.

Treat visit lists (Lookout, Tracker) as weaker than alignment or exact-role results; a visit list can be consistent with a Yakuza frame or a block, so demand a checkable result before a Guilty vote, but also check whether the demand itself is a tactic used by the Yakuza.

Watch for private-message clusters around trials: several players repeatedly PMing one suspect during their trials and then pushing the same Innocent or hold stance is a strong Yakuza tell, and the Yakuza can be hidden among those who insist on 'checkable results'.

Role-blocking a Medic or Sheriff on the night they act is an effective way to kill a claimant, since blocked claims produce no result and become unverifiable; pair it with the Katana on the same target to remove both the claim and the protector.

Keep the Katana holder's identity and holding plan consistent across nights and announce them in the same way publicly, since a Yakuza who holds the Katana at end of night can appear Good to Sheriffs and avoid investigation.

Avoid repeating the same block/Katana target every night. Blocking a Sheriff and Katana-hitting the same player three nights running gave the Village a visit trail (Lookout saw my visits on Carol). Vary targets and keep visits off the Lookout's watch when possible.

Do not use private messages to pressure Village players into specific votes during trials. Private messages are visible as a count to everyone, and repeated PMs from two Yakuza to the same players, plus pushes to vote Innocent, made the pattern obvious and got both of us hanged.

When a visit or block is exposed, do not flatly deny it and then admit it later. The denial-then-admission looked like a lie to everyone and was the basis for the Day 4 trial. Pre-decide a truthful, minimal account (e.g. 'I acted on Carol, nothing more') and stick to it.

Visit lists (Lookout, Tracker) show who visited, not what they did or whether they are evil. Arguing a hanging from visit lists alone is weak, and so is defending someone on that basis. Ask for results that test alignment, and name what the visit could have been for before voting.
Long repeated pleas in public chat and many one-to-one PMs in the same day are read as coordination. Keep public posts short and concrete, and keep private messages rare and disclosed as needed.
Private messages are visible as metadata to the whole table, so a steady stream of PMs from one player to a suspect is itself a read. Avoid repeated private pushes for a vote; make the case publicly.
Treat a Lookout or visit list as a visit record, not an alignment. Ask what the visit was for before hanging someone on it, and remember that a visit can be a block, a protection or a harmless check.

Before voting Guilty on a player whose claim is untestable, ask for one checkable result. Hanging a Village player on a list of contacts left the Yakuza and Village in the same position, and it cost us the Village majority.

A Vulture needs to survive to a Day start with 2 or fewer alive. Avoid voting with a bloc that will nominate you; track who has voted Guilty together and whether a third party is needed to make a majority.
Check the speaking budget and the nomination threshold each Day. With 4 alive, 3 Yes votes nominate and 3 Guilty votes out of 4 hang, so a two-player bloc is enough to hang anyone.

Vary protection targets and protect yourself or a confirmed-trusted Village player rather than the same claimed Sheriff every night; a Pharmacist who learns the pattern will block you. Track role-block risk by asking whether a blocked night left your protection absent, and keep a token in reserve for a later self-protection when the Katana is active.

Treat visit lists (Lookout) as weak evidence against the visitor, since a visit can be a protective or harmless action; prioritise checkable alignment results (Sheriff, Seer) and verify claims before hanging, especially when a town-wide stall hides the real Sheriff's result.

Watch for a self-nomination or early push with no evidence and for private-message clusters between a few players during trials; these were strong Yakuza tells here. Ask for a concrete, testable reason before voting, and don't let a shared stall on claims pass unchallenged.

Once a Yakuza-linked player is exposed, check the private-message network before hanging others; repeated PMs during trials mark both partners, so hang on that pattern only after asking the target what was discussed and whether it was a night action.

Remember that a role-blocked action spends no tokens and leaves no visit, and that a Katana attack on a Standard-protected target fails; use these facts to decide whether a claimed protection or investigation actually happened before trusting the claimant.

Coordinate the Katana and role-blocks so the holder is not a target. Keep a clean record of which Yakuza visited whom, since Lookouts and Trackers reveal visitors to Village and a visible block is a strong tell.

Avoid private messaging a teammate during trials, since every PM sender and recipient is publicly announced. Frequent PM pairs with one player are exposed as a pattern and get used as nomination evidence.

Visit lists alone are weak evidence, but they are checkable. Push for alignment-revealing results or Lookout/Tracker-based corroboration before voting, and avoid pleading for innocence on visit-list cases, which reads as defending a teammate.

Track self-claims against the night log. Claims contradicted by public results (e.g. a Medic protection that a Katana beats) should be weighed heavily, and early nominations that push a Sheriff without evidence are a classic Yakuza signal.
Use the puppet token to silence a Village voice on a day when the Village is about to hang a Yakuza, rather than holding it for a later day that may never come.

Spending a token to clean a player only pays off if they actually die that night; the clean attempt on a surviving or protected target is wasted. Coordinate clean attempts on a target the Yakuza are sure to kill, or hold tokens until a death is likely, rather than burning them on a target who gets protected.

Avoid long private chat plans that are repeated verbatim across nights; the Yakuza chat was fully visible in the revealed log and private DMs between Yakuza members were heavily exposed through Lookout visit lists. Keep private coordination minimal and avoid repeatedly PMing a fellow Yakuza during Village trials, since a PM pattern is an easy tell.

Do not deny a visit that a Lookout can verify; a verified visit contradicted by denial is the fastest way to get a player hanged. If a visit is exposed, admit it immediately with a plausible non-blocking explanation instead of flat denial.

Trials decided on visit lists and private chats alone were repeatedly used to hang Village players; demand a checkable alignment or role result before voting Guilty, and treat unsupported self-nominations and early-stall pushes as the main early suspicion signal.

Track who PMs whom: heavy private contact between two players who later both vote the same way, combined with a shared push for Innocent votes, is a strong Yakuza pair signal, and Village should weigh it earlier than trials on visit lists.

Treat a player who pushes hard without evidence and then nominates themself, asking to be hanged as a 'test', as a likely Jester. Vote Innocent. Hanging a Jester hands them a win and triggers a revenge kill on a random Guilty voter, which could hit a key Village role.
evidence: Frank pushed Carol all of Day 1, self-nominated on Day 2 and said 'If you want a real test, vote Guilty'. All 11 players voted Guilty. The revenge happened to kill Mallory, a Yakuza, but it could just as easily have killed Ivan or Bob.

tip: Never announce your protection target publicly or by private message, and don't protect the same claimed player in the same predictable way every night. Spend Strong tokens on the nights a confirmed investigator is most likely to be hit. Dying with tokens unspent wastes them.
evidence: Ivan said in public and by private message that he would protect Carol again on Night 3. Grace role-blocked Ivan and the Katana killed Carol. Ivan died on Night 4 with both medic tokens unused.

tip: Never flatly deny a night visit that a Lookout or Tracker could have seen. Have a plausible cover role or explanation ready before Day starts. A denial followed by a reversal is far more damning than the visit itself.
evidence: Grace said 'I did not visit Carol on Night 2' after Bob's Lookout result named her. A few turns later she admitted it. That contradiction was the core of the case that hanged her on Day 4.

tip: Everyone can see who sends private messages to whom, so plan in the night chat rather than by private message during the Day. Avoid publicly defending or voting Innocent for a teammate who is under heavy evidence. If a teammate is doomed, distance yourself; don't tie your fate to theirs.
evidence: Judy and Grace messaged each other privately on Days 1, 3 and 4. Judy voted Innocent on Grace and then sent private pleas to Heidi, Erin and Dave. Erin asked how a Vanilla Villager knew about Grace's Night 2 visit, and Judy was hanged on Day 5.

tip: Keep the Katana on the teammate most likely to be investigated, because the holder reads Good to alignment checks. Pair it with blocking the known protector, so the investigator's own check misleads the Village even if they die.
evidence: On Night 3 Grace held the Katana while Carol checked her, and the result was Not Evil. In the same night Grace blocked Ivan's protection, and the Katana killed Carol.

tip: Claiming before you have a result only paints a target. Hold your claim until you have a result worth sharing, or until claiming saves you from a hanging. If you do claim, ask for protection quietly rather than broadcasting your role.
evidence: Carol claimed Sheriff on Day 1 with nothing to show. The Yakuza blocked her on Nights 1 and 2 and attacked her twice, and she never produced a usable result. Alice's public Oracle claim on Day 2 got her killed and cleaned that night.

tip: If the last known Yakuza dies and the game doesn't end, a non-Village Neutral is still alive. Count the players and look hard at whoever has the weakest or latest claim. Be careful about hanging a claimed Cardinal: their death kills a random Good player and can hand a Vulture or other Neutral their win.
evidence: After Judy died the game continued, so a Neutral was alive. Heidi nominated Erin, the claimed Cardinal. Hanging Erin would have triggered a Divine Attack on a random Good player and left 2 alive, enough for the Vulture to win. Bob voted Yes on Erin, but Dave and Erin blocked it, and Heidi was hanged after a late Vanilla claim.

tip: When steering toward your win condition, claim a role early and plausibly and let others lead the pushes. An unclaimed player who suddenly makes an aggressive nomination in the endgame becomes the obvious odd one out.
evidence: Heidi went quiet and gave no role until pressed. She nominated Erin on thin grounds and promised to wait for Bob's Day 7 result before switching to Vanilla. All three remaining players hanged her on Day 6.

tip: Audit a suspicious player's token count only after confirming the role's token totals; a Philanthropist gift or a Medic's spent token changes the count, so read the total as a snapshot, not a role confirmation.

When two claimants contradict on visits, check whether the list was assembled after public claims (timeline) and whether any living player's private result can be mechanically tested before voting; a sole unverified result or a long visitor list is not decisive.

Before a trial, write down the exact count needed and who would be left; late in the game with 3 alive, a single Yakuza vote flip decides, so track who has been consistent with prior votes rather than trusting claims.
Keep Yakuza claims and votes consistent across night chat and day chat; a teammate who votes Innocent on a flipped teammate while nominating the Village's targets exposes the whole bloc.
Check whether a Surveyor or Diviner claim respects its token limit before publicly relying on it; a claim with more survey results than the role allows is an immediate, checkable contradiction.
Keep alignment checks, exact-role checks, and visit reports separate. Framing can alter an alignment result, but it does not change someone’s role or their visit history.

Make frames support a plausible public story, but remember that framing requires a visit and can expose you to visit-based roles. A framed result is a temporary false lead, not proof that will survive a role flip.

Plan Katana attacks around attack and defense levels: a Standard Katana attack fails against Standard Defense, while a Strong attack beats it. Coordinate the holder and target by majority, and account for role-blocks before settling the plan.

applies_to: Fabricator and other roles that can forge information
tip: Spend a limited forgery only when the target is plausibly likely to die that night and the replacement will can redirect suspicion credibly. Avoid making the forged detail so pointed that it looks like an opponent’s agenda.

Treat a confirmed visit as evidence of presence, not proof of a kill or role. Combine it with confirmed flips and mechanics, and keep conclusions conditional when a living player’s claim is the key assumption.
A visit report establishes who visited, not who attacked. Track every plausible visitor—including forced visits—and separate confirmed roles from unverified claims before narrowing the killer pool.

Choose a cover that fits your observable mechanics, but don't rely on it to explain away a verified visit. An Ex-Con claim can explain an Evil Sheriff result, yet its forced visit does not distinguish you from the attacker.

Before choosing a target, consider how simultaneous attacks and the resulting deaths or wills will shape the next day's evidence. A kill can remove a threat but also leave a public trail that makes the remaining visitor pool easier to solve.

When opponents use a claimed role to eliminate themselves from suspicion, challenge the claim's verification rather than simply saying the deduction is uncertain. Offer a specific alternative explanation for the evidence and keep the claim-holder in the candidate pool.
Check the chronology of claims: a specific result stated before the named players claim their actions is stronger evidence than later confirmations that could have copied public information.

When a confirmed Lookout catches all visitors on a night-kill victim, track each visitor's flip. As roles are revealed, the remaining unaccounted visitors strictly isolate the killer, enabling deterministic execution.

When fake-claiming a token-limited role like Surveyor, keep track of official token limits. Reporting three results on a 2-token role creates an unforced mechanical contradiction that exposes the fake claim.
Never cast a lone Innocent vote on a doomed teammate unless you have the votes to save them. The voting record on flipped teammates is the primary trail Village uses to hunt down surviving evil.

A visit report establishes who visited a target, not what they did or which visitor caused a death. Treat it as a candidate list, then narrow it using confirmed flips and independently verified information; don't call the remaining visitor guilty until the alternatives are actually ruled out.

A contradiction between two claims proves at least one account is false; it does not identify which claimant is evil. Before a guilty vote, compare both claimants' incentives and consider neutral roles, Roleplayer false results, and other mechanical explanations.

Use scarce shots on a mechanically grounded suspect, such as a meaningful claim conflict combined with other evidence—not on behavior alone. Match attack strength to the target's likely defense: a stronger-than-needed attack can waste tokens that might decide a later night.

An Evil result is not the same as a Yakuza result. Check appearance exceptions: Ex-Con appears Evil, a Fabricator can frame someone for that night, and Serial Killer appears Not Evil to the Sheriff. State what the result proves—and what it doesn’t.

Keep direct observations, role claims, and deductions separate. A Lookout list can put a killer among a set of visitors, but it does not identify which visitor attacked; verify the timeline before calling later claims corroboration.

Don’t assume a role is unique unless its rules say so. Conversely, a duplicate claim is not proof that either claimant is lying; seek independent evidence such as revealed roles, token limits, or mechanically incompatible actions.

Treat claims and vote patterns as evidence, not confirmation. Roleplayers can receive plausible false investigative results, and Jesters benefit from being hanged, so an apparently bad result or a guilty vote needs context.

Share enough information to let others test your case, but be mindful that private-message contents are visible to recipients and message activity is public. Coordinate around specific claims and timelines rather than building a case from private-message volume.

When fake-claiming a token-limited role like Surveyor (2 tokens), never provide more reports than the role mechanically possesses; town will immediately catch the token count discrepancy once multiple days elapse.

Before a trial, ask whether the nominee gains from dying. A Jester wins when hanged, and Heidi pushed hard for her own hanging, which drew a unanimous Guilty vote. Jester revenge then killed Ivan, a Guilty voter. Check Jester and Executioner incentives before a unanimous hang, and avoid visible Guilty votes on a suspect who is clearly pushing for death.

Check every claimed role against its mechanical limits. Surveyor has two tokens, so three group results cannot be a literal Surveyor. Judy's claim collapsed on that point. A fake role claim should keep its results within the role's token limits and visit rules, or the table will catch it.

Weight a visit list by when its names were predicted. Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj as Alice's visitors before any of them spoke, which is much harder to fake than a list assembled after public claims. Prefer predictions made before the named players commit over lists built from the table's existing claims.

Keep private messages and coordinated scripts minimal. Judy and Mallory's PM cluster and matching Innocent votes made Judy the visible target once Mallory was exposed. Give teammates different wording and avoid triangles that the Village can map.

applies_to: Anyone making a false role claim
tip: Keep a running ledger of that role’s limits, tokens, visits, and result timing. A claim that exceeds a hard limit—such as using more limited actions than the role allows—can undo an otherwise convincing bluff.

Treat a role drawn from a group as probabilistic evidence, not an identity confirmation. Track which players were eligible and how likely each was to produce the result before using it to clear or accuse someone.

Agree on one concise, final night plan: Katana holder, target, and each member’s separate action. Confirm the settled plan once, then avoid contradictory revisions that create execution errors or leave teammates uncertain.

Separate what a result establishes from what it merely suggests. A visitor list can prove someone visited a target, but not that they attacked; account for all plausible visitors and effects before treating the list as a solved deduction.

Role-blocking a Medic only matters if they are the one protecting the Katana target; check protection claims before spending the block, and coordinate blocks with the Katana attack so both land on the same night.

Avoid long repetitive confirmation loops in Yakuza chat; agree targets once with explicit names and roles, and record each member's Diviner or Surveyor result privately so public claims can be kept consistent.

Do not make false public claims that conflict with your own private knowledge of nights; a fake Medic claim on a visited target gets exposed by a flip, and inconsistent Surveyor reports (more groups than tokens) are easy to catch.

Watch for trials decided by a single contested investigative claim; the town repeatedly hanged its own reads (Heidi, Bob, Judy) on unverified results, so demand a checkable detail and avoid tying your vote to one party's narrative.

Track Katana holder and token counts carefully: a Katana holder who dies passes the Katana, and Jester revenge or Serial Killer attacks can kill players at night, so count deaths and visits when evaluating a Lookout or Tracker claim.

When someone claims a result that cannot be true, first check whether an information role could have seen or deduced it before the claim was made. A result that predicts facts before they become public is strong evidence; a result that merely repeats public claims is weak.

Use your role-blocker and killer together. Role-blocking a likely protector can make a kill land, and framing or forging a will can send the town after the wrong player the next day. Coordinate who blocks, who kills, and whose will gets forged in the same night plan.

Write down exact vote counts and timing. Who voted Guilty before a role was revealed, who joined a wagon late, and who defended a confirmed evil player are often more reliable than emotional reads during the day.

If you are repeatedly role-blocked, treat that as information: someone thinks you are dangerous. Protect confirmed or highly likely Good players, and consider self-protection once evil has reason to kill you.

Don’t make your cover claim too convenient. A fake role that explains one suspicious fact can still collapse later when another confirmed result or flip boxes you in. Stay flexible and avoid overcommitting to a story that requires everyone else to misread the mechanics.

If an Executioner's possible target died at night, an Executioner-turned-Jester may be in play. A lone, uncorroborated claimant who contradicts a well-supported report and seems eager to be tried is a Jester candidate. Don't pile on Guilty. Leave them alive, or at least keep the Guilty votes to the bare majority, because the revenge hits a random Guilty voter.
evidence: Heidi (Jester, formerly Executioner on Alice) fake-claimed Tracker 'Grace→Dave', nominated Grace, and stuck to her story. The town hanged her 11-0, giving her the win, and her revenge killed Prosecutor Ivan, whose prosecution tokens were never used.

applies_to: Lookout, Tracker and other visit-based investigators
tip: Post your full visitor list before the visited players claim. Naming players before they explain their visits is the strongest proof a real watcher has, so point it out explicitly when you are challenged. Then use flips to eliminate names until only the killer is left.
evidence: Grace named Carol, Mallory and Niaj before they spoke. Dave's timeline correction flipped the Grace trial and the later Heidi trial. On D4, Bob, Mallory and Frank had flipped and Niaj was confirmed Medic by Mallory's Pharmacist flip, so only Carol was left as the SK.

tip: Never fake a role that a living Village player is likely to hold and counterclaim, and never fake a token role beyond its token limit. If you visited a watched target, a cover like 'Vanilla, no action' isn't available. Pick a claim that has no living counterpart, or one whose results can't be checked.
evidence: Mallory's Medic claim ran into Niaj's real Medic claim. Bob's Sheriff claim ran into Frank, who checked him and got Evil. Judy claimed Surveyor and reported three results from a two-token role. Her late switch to Roleplayer convinced nobody, and she was hanged D5.

tip: Don't vote as a block. Once one teammate flips, every shared Guilty or Innocent vote becomes the town's case against the rest. When a teammate's trial is clearly lost, it can be better to vote Guilty with the town.
evidence: Bob, Judy and Mallory all voted Guilty on the real Lookout Grace and No/Innocent on Bob. After Bob and Mallory flipped, Dave and Erin cited exactly these votes to hang Judy.

tip: Once the Medic is identified, have your role-blocker block them every night you attack a protected-looking target. Also expect a neutral killer to be hunting the same loud information roles. Spread your attack to a second high-value target so both kills don't land on the same player.
evidence: Mallory blocked Niaj on N2 and N3, which stopped his Strong protections on Grace and Frank. But Carol's SK attack hit the same target both nights, so the Katana added no extra kills and the Village kept its numbers.

tip: Shoot the player a confirmed or near-confirmed report places on a victim, especially when that player is one of two people claiming the same role. A Basic shot (1 token) kills most roles, which have no Defense. Save the rest unless you suspect a Neutral with innate Defense.
evidence: Erin shot Mallory, who was on Grace's list and the duplicate Medic claimant. She was the Pharmacist and the Katana holder. It worked, but Erin spent all 3 tokens on a Strong shot when Basic would have done.

tip: When two players claim Sheriff and share a result on a player who flipped Good, the shared result confirms neither of them. Break the tie with an independent check of one claimant, and look at who visited the framed player.
evidence: Bob and Frank both said Alice was Evil. Alice had been framed by Bob, which is also why she read Evil. Frank's N2 check on Bob (Evil) plus Bob's Guilty vote on Grace got Bob hanged, and he flipped Fabricator.

tip: Treat the two numbers as an unordered pair of aggregate counts, not as clues identifying players or actions. Keep a short list of plausible visit patterns that could produce them, and use the result to check a specific hypothesis only when other evidence narrows the possibilities.

applies_to: Village investigators and anyone evaluating their results
tip: A reported visit does not identify the action or the Katana holder by itself. For a Lookout watching a death target, account for the Lookout's own hidden visit; only infer the Katana holder after ruling out other visitors mechanically, not just because one reported visitor looks suspicious.

When a player offers a mechanical explanation for a contradiction—such as a role-block—check whether they stated the relevant facts earlier and whether the explanation fits their other claims. A possible mechanic is not proof that it happened; press for a consistent chronology and seek independent checks.

After a Yakuza flips, promptly compare the vote ledger and private-message links. Treat players who repeatedly defended or voted Innocent with the flipped player as a priority group, then distinguish coordinated defense from ordinary caution using later evidence.

Conserve alerts for nights when visitors are plausible, rather than spending them on several quiet nights in a row. Alert gives only Standard Defense, so it will not stop a Strong attack such as an Arsonist ignition, and an Astral attack does not trigger your visitor attacks.

A Lookout's visitor list excludes the Lookout's own visit, so a reported visitor is not automatically the attacker. Combine the report with independent evidence about who visited and the Lookout's revealed role before concluding who held the Katana.

Compare claimed roles against the exact action rules and earlier claims, then check that against the vote ledger. A claim that explains one result can still have a concrete contradiction elsewhere; here, Niaj's Ex-Con claim conflicted with his earlier 'no night action' claims and he flipped Yakuza.

After a faction member flips, review private-message links and vote patterns together. Treat them as leads rather than proof: repeated coordination can expose partners, but a shared Innocent vote or a PM alone does not establish alignment.

Protection gives no feedback, so track which nights your protected player was attacked by the same Katana chain; a Medic who is killed on Night 1 cannot shape the rest of the game, so consider protecting self on early nights if the Katana is likely aimed at you.

Lookout and Tracker visit reports are hard evidence only for the target's visitors; a watcher never sees their own visit, so a 'sole visitor' claim cannot identify the Katana holder unless you can also rule out the watcher.

Keep the Katana holder's visits minimal and avoid private PM pairs on the same talking points as teammates; the village found the Ivan-Olivia PM cluster and the repeated identical votes were what turned the late game.

A claimed Ex-Con or no-action role that later gets a visit or Tracker result contradicting it is very hard to defend; pick claims whose visits can be explained by the public record and avoid wording like 'no night action' that a tracker can contradict.

Repeated self-nominations by a player claiming Jester are a real risk for the Village, but a Guilty vote on a claimed Jester gives the Jester a win; when the only evidence is a bait pattern, a Jester-revenge hit is worse than one missed hang, so do not let a self-nominator force the execution.

applies_to: Investigators and everyone evaluating alignment results
tip: Treat an Evil result as a lead, not a faction verdict. Check the role’s appearance exceptions and consider frames and Neutral roles; look for independent evidence before spending a trial on the result.

applies_to: Lookouts, Trackers, and anyone interpreting visit reports
tip: Separate “visited the target” from “made the attack.” A Lookout visits their target but cannot see their own visit in the report. Combine reports with independently verified visits and flips before identifying an attacker.

Compare a claim against the rules and the player’s earlier wording. Ask for exact actions and timing, then check whether later explanations fit prior results; a plausible exception, such as a role-block, is not confirmation by itself.

Keep a vote ledger, including nomination votes and trial votes, and reassess it after flips. A vote can be strategic or deceptive, so use patterns as supporting evidence rather than treating any single vote as proof.

Use private-message metadata and repeated voting coordination as prompts to investigate, not as proof. At low player counts, explicitly map which factions or threats must still be alive and compare that constraint with each player’s claims and behavior.

A cover action can explain a visit, but it does not rule out also holding the Katana. Repeating the same holder on several nights when the Katana victims are watched can turn that cover into a pattern; consider rotating the holder when suspicion builds.

A Lookout does not see their own visit, so a report naming one other visitor cannot by itself identify the Katana holder. Combine it with independent visit evidence and revealed roles before drawing that conclusion.

Do not flatly deny a visit that an investigator may have seen. Separate what is established (you visited) from what is inferred (you attacked), and keep any claimed role and action consistent with the mechanics.

An Evil Sheriff result is ambiguous, but not meaningless. Keep the target under scrutiny, and do not treat a Vanilla claim as an explanation; seek independent evidence rather than either convicting or clearing them on the result alone.

Check attack and defense levels strictly: a Standard Katana attack cannot beat Standard Defense. If a competing faction may have innate Defense, plan around a stronger attack or another route to a kill.

When presenting a Lookout report identifying the sole visitor to a kill victim, proactively address the mechanics of your own visit: state upfront that watching is a visit omitted from your own report, and present corroborating evidence (like other investigators' tracks or earlier verified reads) before suspects exploit the self-omission loophole to muddy the case.

When a suspect caught visiting a death victim initially issues a flat denial of visiting and only pivots to an investigative or audit role claim after being named, treat the sequence of statements as a massive scum tell: genuine information roles explain their visits immediately rather than denying them first.

Prioritize watching openly claimed high-value investigative roles like Trackers or Sheriffs rather than unconfirmed quiet players, as surviving investigative roles are primary night kill targets for the evil faction.

Keep a night-visit ledger and account for every role’s mechanics. A Lookout does not see their own visit, so a visitor list alone may not identify the attacker; combine it with independent tracking and confirmed role flips before calling a conclusion certain.

applies_to: Investigators and anyone evaluating their claims
tip: Treat alignment results as appearances, not faction verdicts. Ex-Cons, neutrals, frames, and the Katana’s alignment effect can explain results; ask what each result rules out, then seek independent corroboration rather than either convicting or dismissing it outright.

Track nomination votes separately from trial votes. Voting Yes can simply mean wanting a defense or more information; use the revealed Guilty/Innocent ballots, repeated patterns, and changes in stated reasoning to evaluate alignment.

Use visible private-message metadata as a lead, not proof. Repeated messaging can point to coordination, but check it against public claims, voting behavior, and mechanical evidence before acting on it.

Recalculate the win conditions from all living players and factions instead of accepting an opponent’s proposed shortlist of suspects. Account for neutrals, faction-specific victory conditions, and how each possible execution or night kill changes the end state.
Standard Defense does not protect against Divine Attacks; beware of evil roles like the Ritualist guessing your exact role in the endgame when roles are easily deduced by elimination.
Time your ignition carefully with respect to faction counts; wiping out majority Village while leaving multiple Yakuza alive hands control and coordination to the mafia team.

In a 4-player endgame featuring a known Jester, the remaining players' alignments and roles can often be solved completely by process of elimination; expect opponents to deduce your identity immediately.

Give the Katana to the member whose OWN role action already provides a plausible cover visit to the target, and agree on that cover story before acting. Erin survived a genuine Lookout chain for three days because her 'Accountant audit' justified every visit to Peggy/Dave/Frank. Hiding the victim (Mortician) conceals roles but not Trackers; a cover ACTION conceals the visit itself.

Unanimous Katana votes matter more than clever role tricks. The team locked holder+target every night; with 3-4 alive one missing vote cancels the kill and exposes your top member as the crippled shooter. When one Yakuza proposes a split (Niaj's 'move it to me, hit Alice'), the others should immediately converge rather than 'discuss' — a split vote is a lost attack AND a tell.

A single Evil alignment result plus a 'role that reads Evil' claim is the Yakuza's best hiding place, and it can be exposed by wording. Niaj's 'Ex-Con has no night action' contradicted the role's automatic visit. Require a SECOND, independent result before voting Innocent; treat ambiguity as 're-check tonight', not 'cleared'. The town's tolerance kept a real Clerk alive one extra trial.

A real Lookout's blind spot (it never sees its own visit) is a Yakuza's best shield. Use the visit report as one input, not as the whole case: pair it with the vote ledger (who voted Innocent on the eventual Yakuza flips) and with cross-checks between multiple investigators, instead of re-litigating the same inference twice and hanging the Lookout instead.

Keep a self-declared Jester alive. Judy self-nominated every day and never hung; she absorbed nomination pressure and votes that would otherwise have pointed at Yakuza, and at final 4 she was a guaranteed-non-Yakuza alternative to hanging a teammate. At endgame, do the threshold math (at 4 alive: 3 Yes to nominate, 3 Guilty to hang) and flip one wavering villager rather than hoping.

A Lookout cannot see its own visit, so a Lookout's 'sole visitor' report never identifies the Katana holder unless you can exclude the Lookout; treat such reports as evidence of a visit, not of the attacker.

Repeated self-nominations invite a Guilty vote and get dismissed as bait; a Jester should instead quietly build a real Village-side case with specific mechanical contradictions so a single trial can be won on evidence.

Avoid long private PM sessions between two living teammates in the late game; the Village reads a cluster of PMs and a shared vote pattern as the strongest lead, so vary votes and keep contact minimal.

Before using a Ritualist guess, check whether the target is more likely a Standard-defended Arsonist or Village; a 2-token Divine guess that misses publicly outs the Ritualist and wastes the last tokens.
Track announced trial totals against revealed votes and the living count each day; with few players left, one vote swing decides a hang, so count threshold math before arguing.

Treat a no-visit result as one data point, not a clearance: role-blocks can cancel actions, and some abilities are Astral or passive. Choose follow-up targets that can distinguish between the plausible explanations.

applies_to: Lookouts, Trackers, and everyone evaluating visit reports
tip: When attributing a Katana kill from a Lookout report, account for the Lookout's own omitted visit. A reported visitor becomes strong evidence of the holder only when other visitors are accounted for and the Lookout is independently known not to be Yakuza.

After a Yakuza flips, compare their trial votes and defense partners with private-message links and later vote changes. A single Innocent vote or PM is ambiguous; a repeated pattern across players and days is much more useful.

Keep nomination votes separate from trial votes, and weigh a Guilty vote against both the evidence and the cost of giving a Jester a win. Don't let Jester bait distract from identifying the threats that can eliminate the Village.
Avoid heavy daytime PMs that reveal a bloc; keep coordination in the night chat. Visible message counts between two players can expose a team even if contents are secret.
Never let one Yakuza be the sole non-self visitor to multiple Katana victims. Use a second Yakuza with a cover action on the same target, or astral kills, to muddy Lookout/Tracker evidence.

State the exact limits of your information. A Lookout never sees their own visit; an Evil alignment check cannot distinguish Yakuza from Ex-Con, Jester, Executioner, or a frame. Overclaiming 'confirmed' makes you look deceptive when corrected.

Be consistent about your night action from the start. An Ex-Con auto-visits; if roleblocked, that visit is cancelled. If you earlier said 'no night action', immediately clarify it as 'no chosen action/results' before a Tracker's no-visit report makes it look like a convenient late story.

Openly claiming Jester often makes town avoid hanging you, denying your win. To get hanged, act like a low-value Yakuza/Executioner or let someone else build a case; if you claim Jester, give town a reason to risk the revenge (e.g., 'hanging me confirms X').

A Ritualist's Divine guess spends tokens and is Astral, but a correct hit still tells the target the attacker's role; plan the token spend so a hit cannot identify you, or wait until the role-check is needed to win rather than as a routine kill.

A Lookout cannot see their own visit, so 'sole visitor' reports prove a visit happened, not who attacked; treat a Lookout's watch on a Katana victim as evidence of visits only and cross-check with Tracker results.
Do not let teammates repeatedly PM the same village players in ways that look coordinated; the Katana-holder and trial-vote patterns were the main tells that got the team exposed on Day 6.

Repeated self-nominations by one player are often Jester bait; a Guilty vote on a claimed Jester gives a random Guilty voter a Divine revenge, so count the cost of each Guilty vote before you cast it.

Standard Defense (Medic, Arsonist, Serial Killer) blocks Katana attacks; a Divine attack is the only reliable kill through that defense, so track which roles have Standard defense when guessing who can be killed.
Coordinate with your faction before acting, but keep your public conversation separate from private coordination to avoid exposing your team.

An Evil Sheriff result on someone who claims Vanilla (no role that explains it) is a real case. 'Could be a frame or a Neutral' is a possibility, not evidence. Unless someone offers a specific counter-explanation, vote Guilty instead of acquitting unanimously. Save extra caution for claims that actually explain the result, like Ex-Con.
evidence: D3: Olivia claimed Vanilla against Dave's N2 Evil result and was acquitted 0-12 so the room could chase another lead. She was the Ritualist who won the game N6.

tip: A Lookout's report leaving out his own visit only matters if the Lookout himself might be the Katana holder. If the claimant has independent support, treat 'X was the only other visitor to the Katana victim' as near-proof against X. This is especially true when X first denied visiting and then switched to a role claim.
evidence: D3: Frank reported Erin as Peggy's only other visitor. Mallory's track supported his N1 report. Erin denied the visit, then claimed Accountant. She was acquitted 4-8 and a trial was spent on Frank. The Yakuza then killed Dave and Frank. Once Frank flipped Lookout, Erin was hanged 8-1.

tip: Check a claimant's own earlier statements against the mechanics of the role they claim. A role description they keep contradicting is a stronger tell than tone or timing.
evidence: D4: Alice noticed Niaj had repeatedly said Ex-Con meant 'no night action', but the Ex-Con visits automatically every night. His late role-block excuse could not cover that. He was hanged 6-5 and flipped Clerk.

tip: Don't leave the Katana on a member who also visits with their own role every night. Every Lookout or Tracker hit lands on one person. Rotate the holder, or give it to a member with no action, so the kill visits don't all trace back to the same player.
evidence: Erin held the Katana N1-N4 and also used Mortician on the victims. Frank saw her at Peggy and Dave, and Mallory tracked her to Frank. N1, Ivan proposed holding it himself but backed down over Tracker risk.

tip: If a living Lookout or Tracker may have seen your visit, never flatly deny it. Have a fake visiting-role claim ready and give it the first time you're accused. Reversing a denial under pressure makes the later claim look made up.
evidence: D3: Erin said 'I did not visit Peggy,' then switched to 'I panicked, I'm the Accountant.' Frank later used that reversal as proof, and on D5 every speaker cited it.

tip: Never announce that you will spend a token or investigate tonight, and don't ask others to post their targets. Report only resolved results. An announced token spend tells the Yakuza whom to kill first.
evidence: D2: Peggy said she would spend her Seer token that night and asked investigators to post their N2 targets. The Yakuza Katana'd and cleaned her N2, and her result never reached the Village.

tip: You win only alone, so douse the players you suspect are Yakuza, not just vocal Village. If you ignite and wipe out the Village, you are left with Yakuza you can't kill and can't hang. Also remember your Standard Defense doesn't stop a Divine Ritualist guess.
evidence: Heidi doused Frank, Bob, Grace and Alice, never Olivia or Ivan. Her N5 ignite left her alone with two Yakuza and the Jester. Olivia's 2-token Divine guess killed her N6.

tip: Hold your tokens until elimination makes an exact role near-certain. In the endgame, a Divine guess on the last Neutral can win outright through Defense that stops the Katana.
evidence: Olivia kept both tokens through five nights. N6 she deduced Heidi was the Arsonist, since Judy had openly played Jester, and spent 2 tokens. The Divine attack killed Heidi through Standard Defense and ended the game.

tip: When an announced vote total doesn't match revealed votes, treat it as mechanical evidence of a vote-manipulating role, but only narrow the suspect pool to the voters whose ballots could produce the discrepancy. Don't let a confirmed manipulator automatically condemn every other Guilty voter.

Alignment results are weak compared with exact-role or visit results. 'Not Evil' fits Vanilla Villagers, most Neutrals, and a Katana-holding Yakuza; a differing pair tells you only that two players aren't both Good. Use checks to eliminate worlds, not to prove guilt.

applies_to: Medic, Veteran, Vigilante, and other token roles
tip: Don't hoard all tokens until the final night. Spend when you can either protect a claimed investigator, deny a mechanically suspicious claim, or shoot after a vote or claim contradiction has narrowed the target—not on Day 1 tone.

The Katana holder can appear Good to alignment checks, so let the holder keep it while an investigator is alive. Pair it with Mortician cleaning on high-info kills to hide roles and last wills; cleaning is strongest on the night the Village expects results to resolve a claim.

applies_to: Neutrals and anyone with a false claim
tip: If you must fake a role, keep it mechanically consistent: account for all passive results, token counts, and night actions expected by the setup. A missing automatic result or an impossible repeated result is often more damning than tone or vote history.

Once you publicly claim, reassess whether you are the likely attack target. Don’t automatically protect a claimed investigator again: self-protection costs one token and Standard Defense is enough to stop a Standard Katana attack.

Protection gives no confirmation that it stopped an attack. Choose targets from current threats and likely attacker incentives, rather than treating a previous protection choice or a target’s survival as evidence that the choice worked.

An anonymous, randomly sampled role list establishes that those roles appeared in the sample; it does not assign roles to players or provide a complete roster. Use it as a constraint, not as a forced role map.

When announced trial totals differ from revealed votes, first identify the set of voters who could account for the extra vote. Then use each candidate’s stated position and actual ballot to distinguish them; the total alone does not identify the Ballot Stuffer.

When claiming a unique Town role revealed by an Archivist (such as Vigilante), be prepared for an unrevealed real holder to shoot you that exact night; counter-claims with killing power will test claims directly with bullets.

Do not hoard the Puppeteer token until the late game; deploying it on Day 2 or Day 3 to hijack a key Town voice, muddy consensus, or misdirect a pivotal trial can prevent Town from narrowing down the evil pool mechanically.

When an Archivist provides a clean role draw, maintain a public or private grid matching claims to the archive; once every Good role in the archive is claimed, remaining unclaimed players are mathematically boxed into Evil.

Once a Mortician has spent its tokens, Village reasoning shifts: a Katana kill on a claimed Medic gets cleaned, so keep the Mortician's clean-token count in mind before committing a kill on a power role you want hidden.

Claim-based deflection (accusing a Seer of missing automatic results) can be used against you; a Yakuza Vigilante or Puppeteer claim that conflicts with the archive list invites a second check on the same player, so keep claims that the archive cannot contradict.
Count the trial tally against the revealed votes every time; a doubled Ballot Stuffer vote only points to a pair, so don't stake a vote on a one-name read from it.
When a Yakuza holds the Katana and a teammate has a Puppeteer or Vigilante role, sequence which kills happen first so a Vigilante shot cannot cancel your holder's plan on the same night.

Frank-style Sheriff results on Neutral or Katana-holding players read Good or Not Evil; reserve Sheriff checks for players whose visits you can also track, since those results alone cannot separate Village from Yakuza.

Spend the archive token only when the drawn roles can be cross-checked against deaths or claims that night; a single archive draw among 10 players gives only role existence, not who holds which role, so use it to test claims (e.g. Mortician cleanings) rather than to hunt for Yakuza.

Treat claimed Seer/Sheriff results as unverified until the claimant posts every automatic result; a Seer's random pair arrives every night, so a missing N2 pair is a concrete, testable contradiction to press early rather than late.

Before voting Yes on a nomination, check whether your stated threshold matches your vote; I shifted my standard on Day 1 and that inconsistency was used against me, so write down a concrete bar and hold to it.

Mortician cleanings hide roles but reveal that a cleaned role existed; Yakuza who keep cleaning Village roles create a visible pattern, so mix targets or stop cleaning once the Mortician's tokens are nearly spent to avoid a tell.
Lockstep votes and PM pairs across several players are a signal worth tracking across days; compare who pushed each trial and whether their later votes contradicted their earlier reads.

applies_to: Sheriff and anyone interpreting alignment checks
tip: Treat Not Evil as a broad result, not a clearance: it can include Good players, some Neutrals, and a Yakuza holding the Katana. Share the precise result and its limits rather than turning it into a stronger accusation than it supports.

Update your last will as soon as you receive a result, especially at night when you may be killed before speaking again. Include the target, result, and any important caveat so your best information is not lost.

Separate evidence that a role exists from evidence that a particular player has it. An anonymous archive sample does not assign roles, and a cleaned death hides the victim’s role and will; neither confirms a player’s claim.

applies_to: Everyone, especially Seers and people evaluating Seer claims
tip: Track which results are automatic and which require spending a token. Ask promptly about an unreported automatic result, but treat the omission as something to explain—not proof of a false claim. Random pairs can repeat.

Use manipulated vote totals to narrow possibilities, then reassess when a role flips. A doubled ballot can identify a set of possible voters without proving which one; once the stuffer is revealed, don’t keep treating the other candidate as mechanically implicated.

Cross-reference an Archivist's anonymous role list against revealed deaths and active claims. Because the archive samples a high percentage of players, accounting for each confirmed town role can mathematically force unclaimed players into the remaining evil slots.

Whenever a trial total exceeds revealed votes due to Ballot Stuffer manipulation, identify the small pool of players who voted with the inflated count and look for anyone whose public commentary contradicted their secret ballot.

Save alert tokens during the early game when town investigative and protective roles are actively visiting; activate alerts during late-game nights when visiting town roles are dead or depleted and killing roles must strike.
Share each result promptly and keep a dated record. If you forgot to report one, say that plainly: an unreported result can look like a fabricated one even when it was received normally.

Respect what anonymous and cleaned information can—and cannot—establish. An archive sample confirms roles were present, not who held them; a cleaned death does not confirm the victim's role or alignment.
A repeated random result is possible, even when it looks unlikely. Record the full results and their timing, but don't treat an identical pair as proof of fabrication.

Use a mismatched announced tally to identify the possible manipulated ballots, not to accuse everyone in that set equally. Then use each candidate's own statements and votes to distinguish among them.

Shooting a Yakuza-suspect with a Strong shot at night cost all 3 tokens while I was attacked by the Katana the same night; a Vigilante who is the only Village killer should weigh that the Katana holder will likely target the shooter, so shoot only when the kill is worth losing the shot.

Claims of Seer or Archivist that give automatic results should be checked for missing automatic results; a Seer who skips a night's automatic pair is a lie signal, and an Archivist's names-free list can be cross-checked against who is alive and what the Village already knows.

Track which vote-pushers only follow a single pusher; an early lockstep group (Erin and Dave pressing the same target) was a signal that one of them was Yakuza, and recording it on Day 1 would have helped earlier.

Keep a role-claim matrix with exact token counts, night actions, and all publicly reported results. Many wins come from a claimed power role whose numbers don't add up (spent vs. remaining tokens, missing automatic Seer pairs, archive roles that should or shouldn't exist).

When an announced trial total differs from the revealed votes, treat it as hard mechanical evidence. Count the extra votes and note their direction: it proves a vote-manipulating role is among the voters on that side, not necessarily the person whose public stance looked suspicious. Use it to force multiple defenses and prevent the other possible suspect from escaping scrutiny later.

Don't hang a claimed protective or investigative role just because the claim came late or because the player was evasive. Put them on trial for answers, then require a concrete N1 action that can be tested by another role. If no counterclaim and no contradiction exists, prefer Innocent and arrange a night check.

applies_to: Investigative roles (Seer, Sheriff, Archivist, Tracker, etc.)
tip: Post every automatic or non-secret result as soon as you receive it, even if it seems ambiguous. Missing a Seer's free nightly pair, or failing to explain how a Sheriff result fits the Katana/framing exceptions, gives the Yakuza a free mislynch. Keep a public ledger so your later results can be cross-checked.

Keep your public position compatible with your eventual trial vote. A doubled ballot creates a public discrepancy that narrows the possible stuffer to voters on the side with the extra vote; if your stated read then contradicts your ballot, you give the Village a second, independent reason to focus on you.

Treat anonymous role samples as evidence that roles exist, not proof of who holds them. A role-based deduction needs independently established uniqueness or a contradiction; claims and an unlabelled sample alone do not assign roles.

Report automatic results promptly, with the night and whether the pair was chosen or random. A delayed report can look fabricated even when it is genuine, and a clear record makes later comparisons easier.

applies_to: Party Animal and other Village blockers

Separate accurate information from faction identification. A Diviner can provide genuine role information while pretending to be Surveyor, and an enemy can expose a rival killer. Use useful results without rewarding their source with an alignment clear.

Get targets to commit their actions and remaining resources before revealing checks. Prefer tests that distinguish competing roles, such as retained-token audits. Keep investigative targets unannounced, and decide beforehand how to handle a blocked or missing test so it cannot buy indefinite reprieves.

applies_to: everyone, especially protective and blocking roles
tip: Assume private messages may be read by a Wiretap, whose passive access survives role-blocking. Avoid sharing future targets unnecessarily. Someone quoting an authentic private exchange demonstrates information access, not necessarily Eavesdropper status or Village alignment.

Maintain an actual-versus-claimed ledger of tokens, visitors and destinations before choosing actions. Diviner can imitate Surveyor results, but not its token inventory. Spending your last fictional token removes an audit vulnerability while making later visits harder to explain; Fortune Teller totals can expose that mismatch without tracking you directly.

Avoid having every teammate defend and vote to spare the same suspect. A fabricated rescue may buy one day but become powerful association evidence when its author dies. Before rescuing a teammate, calculate whether the votes can actually save them; if not, preserve another teammate's credibility rather than exposing the whole faction.

Blocking your kill target does not suppress protection supplied by somebody else. Once protection is likely, consider blocking the Medic while attacking the valuable target, or blocking the investigator while killing a less-protected player. Reducing Tracker exposure to one destination is useful, but not automatically worth another failed kill.

Count committed votes before promising a nomination or hanging. An Executioner's cooperation is valuable only if you can recruit the remaining majority with a credible public case. Specify nomination versus conviction support, timing and survival conditions; recruit outsiders before announcing the bargain's target, rather than treating three allied votes as a workable coalition.

applies_to: Yakuza dealing with hostile neutrals and Clerk
tip: Evaluate a rival killer's removal by the resulting faction balance, not merely by whether you identified them. Their attacks may temporarily prevent Village from controlling the endgame, although their cooperation is never guaranteed. Make that strategic decision before committing a Clerk rig: once the rival is successfully nominated on a rigged day, an Innocent vote cannot preserve them.

Choose targets for the following night's threat, not just tonight's likely victim: a new trap cannot trigger on its placement night. Replacing an armed trap resets that delay. Once you have a useful armed trap, consider leaving it in place; it persists through your death and role-blocks that suppress new actions.

Maintain separate ledgers for visitors and destinations. Include players who died that night, self-visits, suppressed actions, and astral nonvisits. Use aggregate counts to expose conflicts among claims, but preserve disjunctions: evidence that 'A or B lied' is not automatically evidence against A alone.

Freeze a suspect's claimed action and remaining tokens before revealing an audit. Avoid advertising investigative targets or making the checker unnecessarily predictable. Decide beforehand what each outcome means: a blocked or missing check supplies no clearance and should not automatically purchase another reprieve.

Compare the strongest complete explanations rather than demanding mechanical certainty. A possible alternative is not equally supported merely because it is legal. Combine results, committed actions, revealed allies' interventions, and voting behavior without double-counting evidence; weigh delay against further hostile kills.

Separate information access from faction identity. A Diviner can supply genuine role information under Surveyor cover, and a Wiretap can quote authentic private messages under Eavesdropper cover. Confirming one detail authenticates only that detail—not the claimed role, other reports, or alignment.

Usually consult the archive early, while the living population—and therefore your sample—is largest. Waiting risks dying with an unused token. Report the complete sample, including duplicate roles, but never treat an omitted role as absent or attach a sampled role to a particular player.

Distinguish information access from alignment. A Diviner can supply genuine Surveyor-like role information, and a Wiretap can quote genuine private messages. Before clearing an investigator, ask which hostile roles could produce the same evidence.

Maintain separate lists of distinct visitors and distinct destinations. Blocks remove visits; astral actions do not visit; Medic self-protection does. Under these roles, only the Katana holder can contribute a second visiting destination. Use count contradictions to identify competing false-account possibilities, not automatically to convict one player.

Get suspects to commit their actions and remaining tokens before revealing an audit. Keep planned audit targets private where possible. A blocked audit yields no count—not zero—and blocking its target does not stop an incoming audit. Do not repeatedly spare a suspect merely because a promised test was obstructed.

After a hostile role reveal, revisit that player's favorable results, rescues, and voting allies. Combine those associations with investigative and action evidence without counting correlated facts twice. A mechanically possible innocent explanation is worth considering, but does not make every suspect equally likely or require another reprieve.

Get a player's committed night account before revealing your tracking result when possible. A matching destination corroborates where they went, not their role or alignment. Prioritize checks that distinguish competing explanations rather than merely reproduce an already-public destination.

Your final night's result may arrive too late to enter your will. Preserve completed results every Day, and optionally record your intended next target as explicitly pending before night. Never assume private night results will automatically appear in your death reveal.

Before granting a reprieve for future testing, specify the discriminating result, likely interference, and what happens if the test fails to occur. A publicly identifiable auditor can be blocked or killed. An obstructed test supplies no clearance and should not automatically buy another night.

Maintain separate counts of visitors and distinct destinations. Include self-visits and actions by players dying that night; exclude blocked and astral actions. Use contradictions to identify sets of incompatible claims—not to select one culprit without additional evidence.

Correct information does not establish friendly alignment: a hostile investigator can truthfully expose a rival killer. After role flips, reassess fabricated rescues and repeated voting alliances. Count Medic self-protection as a self-visit, and preserve contradictions as disjunctions rather than assigning guilt prematurely.

Get suspects to commit their actions and remaining tokens before revealing investigative results, but keep intended investigative targets secret. Compare the strength of competing explanations, not merely whether each is mechanically possible. Repeated rescues of revealed teammates, fabricated exculpatory results and suspicious destinations can collectively justify a vote without proving every claim.
